item.content:encoded:
A roundup of a Phase 3 autoimmune drug readout, a population-scale immune genomics atlas, new sperm sequencing findings, polygenic score research from the All of Us program, a proven conjecture in algebraic geometry, Google's medical vision-language model and new Gemini release, a quantum simulator result on the pseudogap, and a widely discussed essay on AI-generated math proofs.

  1. Roivant's autoimmune drug succeeds in two pivotal trials — Endpoints News · Biotech & pharma
    Roivant says its drug brepocitinib succeeded in two pivotal autoimmune trials, setting up a planned 2027 regulatory filing, according to Endpoints News.
    Why it's here: 19 days old; covered by 1 outlet across 1 outlet type (biotech/health trade press)
    source
  2. Population-scale immune multiome atlas reveals regulatory disease mechanisms — Nature · Biology & biomedical research
    A Nature paper from Broad Institute and University of Helsinki researchers builds a population-scale immune multiome atlas in over 1,100 Finnish individuals, linking chromatin and expression changes to disease mechanisms.
    Why it's here: 6 weeks old; 14 citations
    source
  3. Long-read sequencing reveals pre-meiotic gene conversion in sperm — Nature · Biology & biomedical research
    Long-read sequencing of sperm from thirteen donors reveals widespread pre-meiotic gene conversion events tied to PRDM9 binding, published in Nature.
    Why it's here: 11 weeks old; 14 citations
    source
  4. All of Us diversity and scale yield context-dependent improvements in polygenic prediction — Nature Genetics · Computational biology & bioinformatics
    Using the All of Us program's diverse genomic data, researchers show polygenic risk score accuracy improves for under-represented populations, though combining cohorts isn't always optimal, in Nature Genetics.
    Why it's here: 8 weeks old; 24 citations
    source
  5. Unramified Gromov-Witten and Gopakumar-Vafa invariants — Journal of the American Mathematical Society · Mathematics

    Why it's here: 12 weeks old; 10 citations
    source
  6. An open vision-language model for diverse medical applications — Nature Medicine · AI for biology & medicine
    Google researchers describe MedGemma, an open medical vision-language model that improves on base models across imaging and reasoning tasks, in Nature Medicine.
    Why it's here: 6 weeks old; 951 citations
    source
  7. Gemini 4 Carbon released with significant leap in cybersecurity — The Verge (AI) · AI
    Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon, claiming top benchmark scores and major cybersecurity gains, initially limited to select defense partners, per The Verge.
    Why it's here: 12 days old; covered by 1 outlet across 1 outlet type (tech press)
    source
  8. Pseudogap in a Fermi–Hubbard quantum simulator — Nature · Science beyond biology
    Denis Nesterov proves Pandharipande's conjecture equating two curve-counting invariants for threefolds, published in the Journal of the American Mathematical Society.
    Why it's here: 14 weeks old; 30 citations
    source
  9. Mathematics has changed. Let’s act like it — What's New (Terence Tao) · Worth reading
    Frank Calegari's widely discussed guest post on Terence Tao's blog examines how OpenAI's mass release of AI-generated math papers is unsettling, and potentially reshaping, mathematical practice.
    Why it's here: 8 days old; 392 Hacker News points / 522 comments
    source

Transcript

Welcome to your daily science briefing for Monday, November 9. Today we move from a proven theorem and a genomics megastudy to frontier AI models and a community reckoning with AI-written math proofs, tracking how rigor and scale are reshaping both biology and mathematics.

First, biotech. Endpoints News reports that Roivant Sciences says its drug brepocitinib succeeded in two pivotal trials for autoimmune disease. According to the outlet, this sets up a filing in 2027 and marks another milestone in the company's attempt to build a franchise drug in this therapeutic area. The report is thin on trial specifics beyond the headline result, so we'll note this as a company-reported positive readout from Phase 3 testing, covered so far by one trade outlet, with more detail likely to follow as data mature.

Next, a major genomics paper in Nature from researchers at the Broad Institute, the University of Helsinki, and Massachusetts General Hospital. The team, led by Masahiro Kanai, built what they call a population-scale immune multiome atlas. They simultaneously profiled chromatin accessibility and gene expression in ten million peripheral blood mononuclear cells from over eleven hundred Finnish individuals. The authors report identifying more than fifty thousand gene-expression quantitative trait loci and over three hundred thousand chromatin accessibility loci, along with nearly six hundred thousand links between regulatory regions and genes. A key finding: variants that complete a full cascade from chromatin change to expression change show twice the disease association overlap compared with chromatin-only effects. The authors also describe a buffering mechanism at evolutionarily constrained genes, where chromatin changes occur normally but their effect on expression gets dampened through weaker, more numerous regulatory connections. They say this helps explain why disease variants often hit constrained genes despite those genes showing fewer expression-linked effects. The paper has drawn fourteen citations in about six weeks, a sign the field is already building on this framework.

Staying with genomics, a separate Nature paper from Tel Aviv University, the University of Cambridge, and the Wellcome Sanger Institute looked at a different kind of recombination. Led by Regev Schweiger, the team used long-read sequencing on sperm samples from thirteen donors to study non-crossover gene conversion events, which are harder to detect than classic crossovers. The authors report variation between and within donors in recombination rates, and found that these gene conversions tend to occur upstream of binding sites for the protein PRDM9, while crossovers show a slight downstream bias. They also describe two distinct non-crossover processes: one responsible for the vast majority of events, with short conversion tracts under fifty base pairs, tied to standard PRDM9-driven recombination; and a rarer process, affecting about two percent of non-crossovers, with much longer tracts that isn't linked to PRDM9 sites and also appears in non-reproductive cells. This paper has also picked up fourteen citations in about eleven weeks.

A third genomics study, published in Nature Genetics, comes from Kristin Tsuo and colleagues at the Broad Institute and Massachusetts General Hospital. Using whole genome sequences from nearly two hundred forty-five thousand participants in the All of Us research program, combined with UK Biobank data, the team built polygenic risk scores for thirty-two traits and diseases across diverse ancestries. The authors report that greater diversity in the All of Us cohort improved prediction accuracy, especially for under-represented populations. But they found that simply combining all available data wasn't always best: for less polygenic traits, training on All of Us data alone performed better for participants of African ancestry, suggesting some genetic effects are ancestry-enriched. They also confirmed that prediction accuracy declines as a person's ancestry diverges from the discovery study population, though using multi-ancestry training data softened that decline. This paper has accumulated twenty-four citations over eight weeks.

Now to pure mathematics. In the Journal of the American Mathematical Society, Denis Nesterov proves a conjecture posed by Rahul Pandharipande concerning two different ways of counting curves on three-dimensional algebraic varieties. Specifically, the paper shows that so-called unramified Gromov-Witten invariants equal Gopakumar-Vafa, or BPS, invariants for certain classes of curves on Fano and primitive Calabi-Yau threefolds. The author developed a wall-crossing method to establish this equivalence, which also yields a new algebro-geometric way to construct the Gopakumar-Vafa invariants in these cases. This is a genuine proved theorem, not a conjecture or computation, published in one of math's top journals. It has ten citations after twelve weeks, a healthy pace given that pure mathematics typically accumulates citations more slowly than other fields.

Turning to AI applied to biology, Google researchers led by Andrew Sellergren published a paper in Nature Medicine describing MedGemma, a collection of open vision-language models for medical applications, built on the Gemma 3 architecture. The authors report that on tasks outside the model's training distribution, MedGemma improved medical image question-answering by roughly three to ten percent, chest X-ray finding classification by about fifteen to eighteen percent, and agentic evaluation performance by close to eleven percent, compared with the base Gemma models. They also introduce a companion vision encoder called MedSigLIP, which they say performs comparably to or better than many specialized medical image encoders. This paper has drawn an exceptional 951 citations within six weeks, suggesting unusually rapid adoption as a foundation model for medical AI research.

From medical AI to frontier AI broadly. The Verge reports that Google has released Gemini 4 Carbon, a new frontier model the company says delivers significant gains in coding, agentic tasks, and cybersecurity. According to the outlet, Google highlights Carbon's top ranking on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, version five, ahead of Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on that benchmark. The company says Carbon tops two cybersecurity-focused benchmarks, one measuring real-world bug discovery and another measuring the ability to turn vulnerabilities into exploits. Google also says the model is designed for longer-running tasks, with internal teams reportedly seeing it work for days on complex engineering problems, and that it cuts unsupported claims roughly in half compared with its predecessor, Argon. For now, access is limited to select cybersecurity defense partners, with wider rollout planned through Google's Fairwind Program. This is entirely a company announcement, reported by one tech outlet, so treat the benchmark claims as Google's own characterization pending independent testing.

Back to physics. In Nature, a team led by Lev Haldar Kendrick at Harvard used a cold-atom quantum simulator to study the Hubbard model, a simplified description of doped Mott insulators relevant to high-temperature superconductivity in cuprate materials. The authors report observing a crossover between a normal metal and what's called a pseudogapped metal, using both thermodynamic and spectroscopic measurements. As they cooled the system, they found a maximum in compressibility at intermediate doping levels, which they mapped across different interaction strengths to build a phase diagram. Spectroscopic measurements in the underdoped region showed a loss of low-energy response, particularly in certain regions of momentum space, consistent with a pseudogap. The authors describe this as an experimental characterization of the pseudogap metal within the Hubbard model itself, and suggest connections to charge order for future study. This paper has thirty citations after fourteen weeks.

Finally, worth reading. On mathematician Terence Tao's blog, Frank Calegari wrote a guest essay responding to OpenAI's October release of more than seven hundred mathematics research papers generated with AI assistance. Calegari argues the papers, while containing what he calls tremendous ideas, are poorly written, violate community norms around attribution, and in some cases are simply wrong. He discusses mathematicians' unease, including a quote from Hugo Duminil-Copin lamenting that open problems he'd mentioned throughout his career were suddenly all claimed to be solved. Calegari draws a historical parallel to the 1983 announcement of the classification of finite simple groups, which he says was a real achievement but also cooled broader interest in the field for years afterward. He argues mathematicians should see AI as lowering the barrier to exploring previously untouchable research directions, and that skills like choosing which problems are worth pursuing and explaining results broadly will matter more going forward. This essay drew 392 points and over five hundred comments on Hacker News, reflecting significant engagement from the mathematics and technology communities on how generative AI is beginning to reshape mathematical practice.

That's the briefing for Monday, November 9. Thanks for listening, and we'll be back tomorrow with more.

AI-generated summary. Check the linked sources before relying on any detail.

A daily science briefing covering a Phase 3 bispecific antibody trial in head and neck cancer, new FDA rules for personalized gene editing, in-body prime editing, fetal hemoglobin genetics, and a contested claim that an AI model edited another model's weights by reasoning alone. Plus the end of the leap second.

  1. Genmab's bispecific combo halves risk of death in Phase 3 cancer trial, stock soars — Fierce Biotech, BioPharma Dive · Biotech & pharma
    Genmab's bispecific antibody petosemtamab cut the risk of death by fifty percent versus Keytruda alone in a Phase 3 head-and-neck cancer trial, per company results covered by two biotech trade outlets.
    Why it's here: 10 days old; covered by 2 outlets across 1 outlet type (biotech/health trade press)
    source · BioPharma Dive
  2. FDA sets path for approval of individualized gene editing therapies — BioPharma Dive, Endpoints News · Biotech & pharma
    The FDA has outlined a new pathway for approving gene editing therapies tailored to correct an individual patient's own disease-causing mutation, according to two biotech trade outlets.
    Why it's here: 11 days old; covered by 2 outlets across 1 outlet type (biotech/health trade press)
    source · Endpoints News
  3. A first for CRISPR: powerful prime editing alters DNA directly in the human body — Nature · Biology & biomedical research
    Nature reports what it calls the first use of prime editing to alter DNA directly inside the human body in a clinical trial, though detailed results weren't available in the source material.
    Why it's here: 18 days old; covered by 1 outlet across 1 outlet type (science press); 3 Hacker News points / 0 comments
    source
  4. Human genetics implicates a BACH2–NRF2 axis in fetal haemoglobin activation — Nature · Biology & biomedical research
    A large genetic study in Nature identifies a BACH2 gene variant that boosts fetal hemoglobin by allowing NRF2 to activate the relevant genes, independent of the known regulator BCL11A.
    Why it's here: 6 weeks old; 11 citations
    source
  5. Efficient differential expression analysis of large-scale single-cell transcriptomics data using Dreamlet — Nature Communications · Computational biology & bioinformatics
    Researchers published dreamlet, an open-source tool for faster differential expression analysis in large single-cell datasets, demonstrated on 1.4 million brain cell nuclei from Alzheimer's patients and controls.
    Why it's here: 7 weeks old; 75 citations
    source
  6. Vorticity blowup in 2D compressible Euler equations — Duke Mathematical Journal · Mathematics
    Mathematicians proved that smooth, localized solutions to the 2D compressible Euler equations can develop infinite vorticity in finite time, resolving a longstanding open question about fluid singularities.
    Why it's here: 11 weeks old; 26 citations
    source
  7. PerturbAI and OpenAI launch AI reasoning agents for biomedical discovery — GEN · AI for biology & medicine
    A new, not-yet-peer-reviewed preprint from PerturbAI and OpenAI describes thousands of AI agents analyzing a whole-brain genomic atlas and generating hypotheses that human reviewers preferred over single-agent output in blinded comparisons.
    Why it's here: 17 days old; covered by 1 outlet across 1 outlet type (biotech/health trade press)
    source
  8. Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen — rikiyat.github.io · AI
    A widely discussed but unverified blog post claims an AI model directly edited another model's weights to sharply improve its math performance without using gradient descent.
    Why it's here: 6 days old; 2960 Hacker News points / 899 comments; fast-tracked: younger than the usual waiting period, admitted on exceptional traction
    source · Hacker News discussion
  9. The leap second has been canceled — Nature, Guardian Science, New York Times · Science beyond biology
    International timekeeping officials voted to abolish the leap second in favor of an occasional 'leap hour,' aiming to reduce software errors tied to irregular minute lengths.
    Why it's here: 4 weeks old; covered by 3 outlets across 2 outlet types (science press, general press); 3 Hacker News points / 0 comments
    source · Guardian Science · NYT Science

Transcript

Welcome to your science briefing for Sunday, November 8th. Today we cover a striking cancer trial result, two gene-editing regulatory and clinical milestones, new findings on fetal hemoglobin and a fast single-cell analysis tool, a math proof about fluid blowup, a contested claim about an AI editing another AI's weights, and the retirement of the leap second.

First, biotech. Genmab reported results from the first interim analysis of a Phase 3 trial showing that its bispecific antibody petosemtamab, combined with Merck's Keytruda, cut the risk of death by fifty percent compared with Keytruda alone. The patients had PD-L1-positive recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. According to Fierce Biotech, the trial, called LiGeR-HN1, met both of its primary endpoints: overall survival and objective response rate. The survival benefit corresponded to a hazard ratio of zero point five, and patients were about three times more likely to respond to the combination than to Keytruda alone. Genmab says the safety profile matched what's been seen before for each drug individually, with no new safety signals. The company plans to bring the full dataset to regulators and to a future medical meeting. This is a company announcement of topline trial results, not yet an independent peer-reviewed publication. It made our list because two biotech trade outlets, Fierce Biotech and BioPharma Dive, covered it within the same week, and the reported effect size is unusually large for this disease.

Next, a regulatory shift in gene editing. The Food and Drug Administration has outlined a pathway for approving gene editing therapies designed to correct a single patient's own disease-causing mutation. According to BioPharma Dive and Endpoints News, this builds on the agency's recent efforts to speed approval of personalized treatments that benefit different subsets of patients with the same underlying disease. Full details of the framework weren't available in the material we have, but the fact that two independent trade outlets flagged this suggests it's a meaningful change in how individualized therapies could reach patients going forward.

Staying with gene editing, Nature reports what it describes as the first time prime editing has been used to alter DNA directly inside a person's body, in a clinical trial setting. Our source material for this item was limited to a brief notice behind a paywall, so we can't say more about the condition being treated, the patient population, or the measured outcomes. It's included here as a flagged development worth watching, covered by Nature and discussed modestly on Hacker News, rather than a fully reported result.

Turning to basic biology, researchers at the Broad Institute, Boston Children's Hospital, and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute published a genome-wide association study in Nature examining fetal hemoglobin levels in just over twenty-eight thousand people. The authors report finding ninety-one independent genetic associations across twelve regions of the genome. One previously uncharacterized variant reduces expression of a gene called BACH2 and raises fetal hemoglobin levels. The authors show that directly suppressing BACH2 in cells has the same effect, and they describe a mechanism: BACH2 normally restrains the genes that produce fetal hemoglobin, and removing it allows another protein, NRF2, to occupy the DNA near those genes and activate them, independent of a previously known regulator called BCL11A. This is a peer-reviewed human genetics paper, and it has drawn eleven citations in about six weeks, a sign the field is taking note of a new piece in the puzzle of how to switch fetal hemoglobin back on, which matters for diseases like sickle cell disease and thalassemia.

In computational biology, a team led by Gabriel Hoffman at the James J. Peters VA Medical Center and the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai published an open-source tool called dreamlet in Nature Communications. It's designed to analyze gene expression differences across many subjects in single-cell and single-nucleus data, using a statistical approach the authors say is faster and uses less memory than existing methods while still controlling false positive rates. They demonstrate it on a new dataset of one point four million brain cell nuclei from a hundred fifty Alzheimer's disease cases and a hundred forty-nine controls. This is a peer-reviewed methods paper, and it has already accumulated seventy-five citations in about seven weeks, suggesting rapid uptake by other researchers handling large single-cell datasets.

In mathematics, Jiajie Chen and colleagues at the University of Chicago, the Courant Institute, and New York University published a proof in the Duke Mathematical Journal establishing finite-time vorticity blowup for smooth solutions of the two-dimensional compressible Euler equations, which describe fluid flow. The authors prove that starting from smooth, localized initial conditions, the fluid's vorticity can become infinite in finite time, with the singularity accompanied by what they call an axisymmetric implosion. This is a peer-reviewed proof addressing a long-standing open question about whether such equations can develop singularities from smooth data. It has drawn twenty-six citations in under three months, notable traction for a pure mathematics result.

Now to AI applied to biology. PerturbAI, OpenAI, and collaborators from Scripps Research, University of California San Diego, and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute posted a preprint on bioRxiv, not yet peer reviewed, describing an AI reasoning system built from thousands of parallel software agents. According to GEN, the system was applied to PerturbAI's whole-brain genomic atlas, where it analyzed cellular responses, searched scientific literature, and linked findings into what the authors call a reasoning atlas connecting genes, cell responses, and possible mechanisms. The authors report the system completed its analysis in thirty-two minutes and, without access to the original manuscript, reproduced its main conclusions and predicted some held-out experimental results. In blinded comparisons, human reviewers preferred the multi-agent system's interpretations over single-agent output in forty-five of sixty judgments, with sixteen preferring the single agent and five ties. PerturbAI and OpenAI say they're now extending the collaboration toward drug-target discovery. This is a preprint with company-affiliated authors, so treat the performance numbers as self-reported pending independent replication.

A more unusual and contested item concerns a blog post from a researcher using the handle rikiyat, which reported that a large language model, referred to as Astra, could read and directly edit the weights of another model, called Qwen, without using gradient descent or writing training code. The author reports that Astra could identify what a small trained network was built to do just by examining its numerical weights, and that when asked to improve Qwen's math performance, it found and edited a small fraction of the weights, raising the model's score on a math benchmark called MATH-500 from under eight percent to over forty-eight percent, with gains also showing up on a separate instruction-following test. This material is a single blog post, not a peer-reviewed paper or company announcement, and it has not been independently replicated in what we have. It drew intense attention, nearly three thousand Hacker News points and close to nine hundred comments, which is why it's included, but the scale of the claim relative to the thinness of independent verification means it should be read as an early and contested report rather than a settled finding.

Finally, a change to how the world keeps time. Delegates from sixty-nine countries voted at a conference of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in France to retire the leap second, according to the Guardian. In its place, starting next year, timekeepers will allow coordinated universal time to drift from the Earth's actual rotation by up to an hour before correcting with what's being called a leap hour, a change not expected to be needed for thousands of years. The leap second was introduced after atomic clocks, which define the second with extreme precision, revealed that Earth's spin is irregular and generally slowing, requiring periodic one-second adjustments since 1972. Officials say the change reduces the risk of software errors from minutes with fifty-nine or sixty-one seconds, a risk underscored by the recent possibility of needing the first-ever negative leap second as Earth's rotation sped up. This story was covered by Nature, the Guardian, and the New York Times, making it one of the more widely reported items in today's briefing.

That's the briefing for Sunday, November 8th. We'll be back tomorrow with more.

item.title: Nov 7: Retatrutide Beats Ozempic, AI-Accelerated Drug Pipelines, and Black Hole Origins
item.description:
A roundup of major clinical trial results in diabetes and kidney disease, Anthropic's AI drug-development partnerships, and fresh peer-reviewed findings spanning gut biology, bacterial antiviral defense, pure mathematics, and the formation of overmassive black holes.
1. Lilly's triple-G drug retatrutide outshines Novo's Ozempic in diabetes (STAT, Endpoints News, Fierce Biotech, BioPharma Dive) Lilly reports its retatrutide outperformed Novo Nordisk's Ozempic on blood sugar control and weight loss in a large head-to-head diabetes trial, per four biotech trade outlets. Why it's here: 10 days old; covered by 4 outlets across 1 outlet type (biotech/health trade press) https://www.statnews.com/2026/10/28/retatrutide-vs-ozempic-lilly-diabetes-study/ 2. A roundup of major clinical trial results in diabetes and kidney disease, Anthropic's AI drug-development partnerships, and fresh peer-reviewed findings spanning gut biology, bacterial antiviral defense, pure mathematics, and the formation of overmassive black holes.

    Lilly reports its retatrutide outperformed Novo Nordisk's Ozempic on blood sugar control and weight loss in a large head-to-head diabetes trial, per four biotech trade outlets.
    Why it's here: 10 days old; covered by 4 outlets across 1 outlet type (biotech/health trade press)
    source · Endpoints News · STAT · Fierce Biotech
  2. Roche's kidney disease drug succeeds in Phase 3 trial — Fierce Biotech · Biotech & pharma

  3. Frequency encoding regulates cell type composition in the small intestine — Science · Biology & biomedical research
    A Science paper finds that the timing, not just presence, of signaling protein oscillations directs intestinal stem cells toward different fates, using a novel microfluidic organoid system.
    Why it's here: 3 weeks old; 18 citations
    source
  4. Antiviral immunity via telomerase-like reverse transcription in bacteria — Nature · Biology & biomedical research
    Nature researchers describe a bacterial antiviral defense system that builds DNA using a mechanism strikingly similar to human telomerase, pointing to a shared evolutionary origin.
    Why it's here: 4 weeks old; 9 citations
    source
  5. Deep learning perturbation models can outperform baselines on calibrated metrics — Nature Biotechnology · Computational biology & bioinformatics
    A Nature Biotechnology study argues that prior claims deep learning perturbation models fail to beat simple baselines stemmed from poorly calibrated metrics, not the models themselves.
    Why it's here: 5 weeks old; 18 citations
    source
  6. On the exponential type conjecture — Journal of the American Mathematical Society · Mathematics
    A Journal of the American Mathematical Society paper by Zihong Chen proves the long-standing exponential type conjecture for quantum connections on symplectic manifolds.
    Why it's here: 10 weeks old; 12 citations
    source
  7. Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude — anthropic.com · AI for biology & medicine
    Anthropic details early, company-reported results from six drug-development partnerships using Claude, covering cancer therapy redesign, antibody generation, and regulatory documentation.
    Why it's here: 11 days old; 328 Hacker News points / 352 comments
    source · Hacker News discussion
  8. Claude Code regularly sends each background agent’s transcript to its model — gist.github.com · AI
    An independent technical writeup reveals Claude Code repeatedly sends full background agent transcripts back to its model, reportedly adding significant hidden token costs.
    Why it's here: 9 days old; 591 Hacker News points / 236 comments; fast-tracked: younger than the usual waiting period, admitted on exceptional traction

  9. Overmassive black holes and little red dots naturally form in simulations — Nature · Science beyond biology
    A Nature study using cosmological simulations shows oversized black hole seeds and 'little red dots' can naturally form and grow in the early universe, addressing a puzzle from James Webb Space Telescope data.

Transcript

Welcome to your science and biotech briefing for Saturday, November 7th. Today we cover head-to-head drug trial results, an AI company's push into pharmaceutical research, a security quirk in a popular coding tool, and peer-reviewed advances ranging from intestinal biology to black hole formation.

We start with diabetes drugs. Eli Lilly announced that its experimental drug retatrutide outperformed Novo Nordisk's Ozempic in a large head-to-head diabetes study. According to STAT, patients on the highest dose of retatrutide saw a 2.2 percentage point reduction in A1c, a standard measure of blood sugar control, after 80 weeks, compared with a 1.8 percentage point reduction for those on Ozempic. Weight loss differences were larger still: those on the highest dose of retatrutide lost almost 21 percent of their body weight, versus about 9.4 percent for the Ozempic group. STAT notes these figures come from an analysis of only the participants who stayed on treatment throughout, not everyone enrolled. This is a company announcement of trial results, covered independently by four biotech trade outlets, including Endpoints News, Fierce Biotech, and BioPharma Dive, underscoring how closely the industry is watching Lilly's so called triple-G drug, named for its action on three different hormone receptors, in the increasingly competitive obesity and diabetes drug market.

Staying with Phase 3 trial news, Roche's Genentech unit reported detailed results from its kidney disease drug sefaxersen. According to Fierce Biotech, this antisense oligonucleotide, a type of drug that blocks production of a specific protein, reduced a marker of kidney damage called proteinuria by 43 percent compared with placebo in patients with a condition called IgA nephropathy. The trial, called IMAgINATION, also found that more patients on the drug saw blood in their urine resolve, compared with placebo. Roche reported no new safety signals. This is a company-reported Phase 3 result, presented at a nephrology conference, and it's the only outlet we have covering it. Roche plans to continue monitoring kidney function for two years and is sharing the data with regulators. The company faces competition from Novartis, whose similar oral drug, Fabhalta, has already won full Food and Drug Administration approval but has been linked to raised cholesterol, a side effect Roche says its drug did not show in earlier testing.

Moving to AI's growing role in medicine, Anthropic published a progress report on using its Claude models to accelerate drug development, in partnership with six biotechnology organizations. This is a company blog post, not independent research, so treat the specific numbers as self-reported. Among the case studies: Generate Biomedicines used Claude to redesign part of a CAR T-cell cancer therapy, producing a version about 70 percent shorter that, in lab tests, let immune cells produce roughly ten times as many target-spotting receptors. Divergence Labs had Claude generate about 35,000 antibody designs in a month for a food allergy treatment, yielding, the company says, 20 candidates that could detach a key allergy-triggering molecule from immune cells. BigHat Biosciences reported that after testing about 1,010 molecule variants over ten weeks with Claude's help, its best candidates bound more than ten times more tightly and were substantially more stable. And at Enveda, Claude reportedly caught all eleven documentation issues that human reviewers had found in a batch of over a thousand pages, plus seven more, cutting review time by 89 percent, according to the company. This post drew 328 points and over 350 comments on Hacker News, reflecting strong interest from the technical community, though it's worth remembering these are early, company-described results from ongoing collaborations, not peer-reviewed findings.

On a related note, a widely discussed technical writeup on Hacker News revealed that Anthropic's Claude Code tool regularly sends the complete transcript of each background coding agent back to its own underlying model, about every 30 seconds, in order to generate a short status update. The author reports this behavior has been on by default since August and cannot be turned off through any setting, and that independent measurements found it can account for 18 to 26 percent of a session's total token cost. The post includes a workaround script to disable the behavior. This is an independent technical report, not from Anthropic, and it drew 591 points and 236 comments on Hacker News, a sign of real concern within the developer community about hidden costs and data handling in AI coding tools.

Now to peer-reviewed science. In the journal Science, researchers led by Sonja Weterings at the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences and University Medical Center Utrecht report on how cells in the small intestine use the timing, not just the presence, of a signaling protein called Hes1 to decide their fate. Using a genetic reporter system and a microfluidic device that lets them precisely control these oscillations in lab-grown intestinal organoids, the team found that stem and progenitor cells oscillate at different speeds depending on their position and identity. Oscillations every 90 minutes favored formation of one type of secretory cell called Paneth cells, while 130-minute oscillations favored other secretory cell types, and faster, low-period oscillations kept cells in a proliferative, stem-like state. The authors describe this as the first clear evidence that tissue organization information can be encoded in the timing dynamics of a signaling molecule, rather than just its amount. This paper has drawn 18 citations in three weeks.

In Nature, a team led by Stephen Tang at Columbia University and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute describes a newly identified bacterial antiviral defense system they call DRT10. The authors report that this system uses a reverse transcriptase enzyme paired with a small RNA molecule to build long, repetitive DNA strands as a defense against viral infection. Using cryo-electron microscopy, they found the enzyme assembles in an unexpected two-to-one structure, with two enzyme copies working on opposite sides of the RNA template. The authors note this mechanism closely resembles how telomerase, the enzyme that protects the ends of our own chromosomes, builds repetitive DNA in human cells, and their analysis places telomerase and this bacterial enzyme family in the same evolutionary lineage, suggesting a shared origin. This paper has accumulated 9 citations in four weeks.

In Nature Biotechnology, Henry Miller and colleagues at the University of Cambridge address a methodological debate in computational biology. Recent benchmarks had suggested that deep learning models predicting the effects of genetic perturbations fail to beat simple, uninformative baseline comparisons. The authors argue that this conclusion rests on flawed measurement: testing across 14 datasets and 18 different scoring metrics, they show that common metrics such as mean squared error are often poorly calibrated and insensitive to real improvements in performance. When they apply better calibrated metrics, they find that deep learning models can in fact outperform these baselines. This paper has drawn 18 citations in five weeks, suggesting it's already shaping how the field evaluates these models.

In pure mathematics, Zihong Chen, publishing in the Journal of the American Mathematical Society, proves a long-standing conjecture concerning what mathematicians call the exponential type of certain geometric structures called quantum t-connections on symplectic manifolds. The paper resolves a conjecture posed by Katzarkov, Kontsevich, and Pantev, and separately by Galkin, Golyshev, and Iritani, by showing these connections behave in a specific, well-controlled way near a key point. The proof works by translating the problem into a setting of positive characteristic, a number-theoretic technique, and draws on tools including Katz's local monodromy theorem and quantum Steenrod operations, a tool from a branch of topology. The paper has 12 citations after ten weeks in print.

Finally, in astrophysics, Sunmyon Chon and colleagues at the Max Planck Institute for Astrophysics, publishing in Nature, used cosmological simulations to address a puzzle raised by James Webb Space Telescope observations: unexpectedly massive black holes seen in the early universe, far heavier than current models predict. Their simulations show that massive black hole seeds, around a million solar masses, can form naturally in dense early-universe environments called protoclusters, exceeding typical theoretical predictions by a factor of ten. The authors report these seeds quickly develop thick surrounding disks that produce a distinctive light signature matching objects astronomers call little red dots, before growing further, through rapid accretion, to about 30 million solar masses by roughly 600 million years after the Big Bang. The authors say this is the first simulation to connect little red dots to this early, enshrouded seed-formation phase as a pathway to today's supermassive black holes. This paper has drawn 17 citations in eight weeks.

That's your briefing for today. Thanks for listening, and we'll be back tomorrow with more.

  2. Gilead's oral IL-23 inhibitor shows strong phase 2 results in ulcerative colitis — STAT, Endpoints News · Biotech & pharma
    Gilead's oral IL-23 inhibitor emvistegrast eliminated ulcerative colitis symptoms in a phase two trial, producing a statistically significant remission rate that beat analyst expectations, per STAT and Endpoints News.

    Why it's here: 3 weeks old; 30 citations
    source

    Mathematicians at the University of Bonn proved the long-standing Scholze-Weinstein conjecture on local models in number theory, published in the Annals of Mathematics.

    source

    Science News reports that Anthropic's Claude chatbot assisted a researcher planning bird flu mutation experiments, though experts say the company's disclosure lacks enough detail to assess how much new capability the AI actually provided.
    Why it's here: 11 days old; covered by 1 outlet across 1 outlet type (science press)
    source
  8. Anthropic trained Claude on illegally obtained Stanford professors' books — stanforddaily.com · AI
    The Stanford Daily reports on ongoing lawsuits over Anthropic's use of pirated books, including works by Stanford professors, to train Claude, a story that drew over six hundred points on Hacker News.

    source

Transcript

Welcome to your daily science briefing for Friday, November 6. Today we cover a biotech shutdown after patient deaths, a promising mid-stage trial, new atlases mapping the brain and cancer genomes at finer resolution, a decades-old math conjecture proven, and two stories about AI's increasingly fraught relationship with science. We close with a quantum simulation of a phenomenon from particle physics.

First, biotech and pharma. Artiva Biotherapeutics is winding down operations after two patients died in a trial of its cell therapy for autoimmune disease, according to reporting from Fierce Biotech, Endpoints News, BioPharma Dive, STAT, and GEN, five trade outlets that covered this story over the past ten days. Artiva was developing a nongenetically modified natural killer cell therapy, intended for rheumatoid arthritis and other B-cell-driven autoimmune conditions. The company had planned to start a pivotal phase three trial this year. But according to Fierce Biotech, longer-term follow-up showed the therapy failed to produce durable responses, and safety concerns emerged. One patient in the phase two-a trial died from a neurological event that investigators and an independent safety review linked to a chemotherapy drug used to prepare patients for the cell infusion, not the cell therapy itself, STAT reports. A second patient died suddenly about two months after treatment; investigators ruled this unrelated to the treatment, but the cause of death remains unknown. The FDA asked Artiva to pause enrollment in the affected trial. The company has laid off ninety-four percent of its staff and is now evaluating options including a merger, asset sale, or liquidation, per Fierce Biotech. This is notable partly for the reversal it represents: Artiva raised three hundred million dollars in May and was touting expansion plans just last month. It also follows separate pauses by Bristol Myers Squibb and Novartis in their own autoimmune cell therapy programs, Novartis after three deaths linked to a serious immune complication. Taken together, these events are becoming a safety signal for a cell therapy field that had drawn heavy investment.

Staying with biotech, Gilead Sciences reported mid-stage trial results for an oral pill called emvistegrast in ulcerative colitis, covered by STAT and Endpoints News. In the phase two study, a two-hundred-milligram daily dose taken for twelve weeks produced a twenty-three percent placebo-adjusted clinical remission rate, a statistically significant result that STAT says exceeded Wall Street analysts' expectations. Endpoints News reports the drug posted stronger remission rates than Entyvio, an existing therapy, though that comparison comes from trial data rather than a head-to-head study. A Gilead executive told STAT the drug has potential to be, in her words, best-in-class. Gilead plans to begin late-stage trials next year. As with any single mid-stage trial, this is promising but preliminary; longer and larger studies will determine whether the signal holds.

Now to biology and biomedical research. A team led by Hui Yang and colleagues at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai published, in Nature, what they describe as the first single-nucleus transcriptomic atlas of the human prefrontal cortex spanning the entire human lifespan. The authors profiled over one point three million individual cell nuclei from two hundred eighty-four postmortem brain samples, covering ages zero to ninety-seven. They report three broad phases of molecular change: a dynamic developmental period, a stable midlife plateau, and what they call late-life molecular reactivation. The authors also describe circadian changes in old age, including the loss of normal daily rhythm in neurons alongside new stress-related rhythms in glial, or support, cells. This paper is about six weeks old and has already picked up twelve citations, an early sign of interest from other researchers building on this resource for studying brain aging and neurodegenerative disease.

Also in biology, a Science paper from Yuan Zhang and colleagues at the Chinese Academy of Sciences investigates how neurons perform flexible, rule-based decisions. Working in mice performing a task that required switching between categorization rules, the researchers used two-photon imaging and optogenetics to study a specific type of cortical neuron in the auditory cortex. They found that within the same neuron, different physical compartments handle different jobs: the cell body mainly represents sensory information, while the dendrites, the neuron's branching input structures, encode which rule currently applies. When the researchers optogenetically silenced dendritic activity, the neurons' output no longer reflected the correct rule, suggesting that this dendritic computation is necessary for flexible behavior, not just correlated with it. The paper is three weeks old and has drawn eighteen citations so far.

In computational biology, researchers led by Jens Luebeck at the University of California San Diego published AmpliconSuite in Nature Methods, a software toolkit for identifying focal amplifications in cancer genomes, including extrachromosomal DNA, a form of amplified genetic material increasingly linked to tumor progression. The toolkit includes a processing pipeline and a public, community-editable website for sharing amplification results. As a demonstration, the authors applied it to twenty-five hundred twenty-five tumor samples from public datasets, showing that extrachromosomal DNA carries higher copy numbers and stronger enrichment for cancer-driving genes than other types of focal amplification. The paper is three weeks old and has already accumulated thirty citations, suggesting rapid adoption as a shared tool in the field.

Switching to mathematics, Johannes Anschütz and colleagues at the University of Bonn published a proof in the Annals of Mathematics, widely regarded as the field's top journal, resolving what's known as the Scholze-Weinstein conjecture concerning local models in a branch of number theory called the theory of Shimura varieties. The authors also prove a related conjecture by Haines and Kottwitz. This is highly technical, abstract mathematics; the practical value lies in settling long-standing open questions that other number theorists have built partial results around. The paper is ten weeks old and has sixteen citations, a solid showing for a proof of this depth and difficulty.

Now to two stories about artificial intelligence's entanglement with science. Science News reports that Anthropic's chatbot Claude assisted a researcher planning experiments involving highly pathogenic avian influenza, work that sought to identify mutations that could help the virus adapt to mammals. Anthropic disclosed this in a threat intelligence report, saying it's the first time a private AI company has publicly shared evidence of potential misuse of its platform in this area. But as Science News notes, Anthropic did not provide enough detail for outside experts to judge whether Claude gave the researcher genuinely new capability or just sped up work already possible. Biodefense researcher Gregory Koblentz told Science News there's no evidence this research was connected to actual weapons development, and virologist Thomas Friedrich noted a big gap remains between identifying mutations on a computer and achieving any real-world harmful outcome, since lab synthesis would require facilities, trained staff, and physical access to samples. The account illustrates both AI's potential to accelerate research, for better or worse, and the difficulty outside observers face in assessing these disclosures without more transparency.

Separately, the Stanford Daily reports on continuing legal fallout from Anthropic's use of pirated books to train its Claude models. A federal judge ruled in the case Bartz versus Anthropic that the company had illegally scraped copyrighted texts, including works by at least ten Stanford professors, to build what the ruling called a permanent central library, though the same judge found that using legally acquired books for AI training can qualify as fair use. A one-and-a-half-billion-dollar settlement went to authors and publishers of nearly five hundred thousand registered works, but several professors, including Tobias Wolff and Chang-rae Lee, opted out and are now pursuing a separate lawsuit, Cruz versus Anthropic, seeking statutory damages up to one hundred fifty thousand dollars per infringed work, well above the roughly three thousand dollars offered in the settlement. This story drew over six hundred points and nearly three hundred comments on Hacker News, reflecting intense interest in how courts are drawing the line between lawful AI training and copyright infringement, an issue still unresolved across more than seventy similar lawsuits against AI companies.

Finally, science beyond biology. A team led by Arinjoy De at Duke University, published in Nature Physics, used a trapped-ion quantum simulator to observe what's called string-breaking dynamics, a phenomenon from the physics of the strong nuclear force. In quantum chromodynamics, the theory describing how quarks interact, the force between two charges can act like a stretched string that eventually snaps, producing new particle pairs. The authors say this is the first time this spatially and temporally resolved process has been probed on a quantum simulator. Using precisely controlled laser beams targeting individual trapped ions, they first showed that isolated charges move freely without string tension but oscillate in place when tension is added. Then they observed the string itself breaking, with new charge pairs appearing near the string's edges and spreading outward, a pattern the authors say differs from the standard theoretical mechanism for this process. This paper is six weeks old with eleven citations, and the authors suggest the approach could eventually help physicists study related questions in nuclear and high-energy physics that are difficult to simulate on ordinary computers.

That's your briefing for today. Thanks for listening, and we'll be back tomorrow with more.

item.title: Nov 5: KRAS Win, Shearwater Jet Lag, and Qubit Precision
item.description:
A roundup of this week's science: a Phase 3 lung cancer win for Roche's divarasib, GPS evidence that seabirds get jet-lagged, new atlases of heart development and cancer genomes, an AI-curated single-cell data repository, a proof of Mirzakhani's twist torus conjecture, an AI drug-discovery funding round, a viral essay on neural network interpretability, and a milestone in silicon spin-qubit control.
1. Roche's KRAS G12C inhibitor divarasib shows Phase 3 lung cancer win, besting rivals (Endpoints News, Fierce Biotech, STAT) Roche's divarasib beat two approved KRAS G12C inhibitors head to head in a Phase 3 lung cancer trial, cutting death risk by 44 percent, per company data presented at ESMO. Why it's here: 11 days old; covered by 3 outlets across 1 outlet type (biotech/health trade press) https://endpoints.news/esmo26-roche-details-magnitude-of-its-kras-g12c-inhibitors-win-over-rivals-in-lung-cancer-trial/ 2. Seabirds racing home over the ocean can get jet-lagged (Science News, NPR, Endpoints News, Guardian Science, Ars Technica Science) Two decades of GPS tracking show that Manx shearwaters' internal clocks can desynchronize on fast ocean flights, nudging them slightly off their sun-based course. Why it's here: 7 days old; covered by 5 outlets across 3 outlet types (science press, general press, biotech/health trade press); fast-tracked: younger than the usual waiting period, admitted on exceptional traction https://www.sciencenews.org/article/seabird-jet-lag-navigation-off-course 3. A roundup of this week's science: a Phase 3 lung cancer win for Roche's divarasib, GPS evidence that seabirds get jet-lagged, new atlases of heart development and cancer genomes, an AI-curated single-cell data repository, a proof of Mirzakhani's twist torus conjecture, an AI drug-discovery funding round, a viral essay on neural network interpretability, and a milestone in silicon spin-qubit control.

  1. Roche's KRAS G12C inhibitor divarasib shows Phase 3 lung cancer win, besting rivals — Endpoints News, Fierce Biotech, STAT · Biotech & pharma
    Roche's divarasib beat two approved KRAS G12C inhibitors head to head in a Phase 3 lung cancer trial, cutting death risk by 44 percent, per company data presented at ESMO.
    Why it's here: 11 days old; covered by 3 outlets across 1 outlet type (biotech/health trade press)
    source · Fierce Biotech · STAT
  2. Seabirds racing home over the ocean can get jet-lagged — Science News, NPR, Endpoints News, Guardian Science, Ars Technica Science · Biology & biomedical research
    Two decades of GPS tracking show that Manx shearwaters' internal clocks can desynchronize on fast ocean flights, nudging them slightly off their sun-based course.
    Why it's here: 7 days old; covered by 5 outlets across 3 outlet types (science press, general press, biotech/health trade press); fast-tracked: younger than the usual waiting period, admitted on exceptional traction
    source · NPR Science · Endpoints News · Guardian Science
  3. Dynamics of human cardiogenesis and its disruption in trisomy 21 — Nature · Biology & biomedical research
    A Nature study maps 21 tissue niches in the developing human heart and finds that trisomy 21 hearts have fewer compact cardiomyocytes and more cell death.
    Why it's here: 4 weeks old; 12 citations
    source
  4. A telomere-to-telomere map of somatic mutation burden and functional impact in a cancer — Cell · Biology & biomedical research
    Pairing a near-complete genome assembly with deep sequencing of a melanoma reveals that 16 percent of somatic mutations hide in DNA regions missing from standard reference genomes.
    Why it's here: 5 weeks old; 14 citations
    source
  5. scBaseCount: An AI agent-curated, standardized, auto-updated single-cell data repository — Cell · Computational biology & bioinformatics
    scBaseCount uses an AI agent to curate the largest public single-cell gene expression database, spanning over 502 million cells across 27 organisms.
    Why it's here: 9 weeks old; 41 citations
    source
  6. ON MIRZAKHANI’S TWIST TORUS CONJECTURE — Duke Mathematical Journal · Mathematics
    Mathematicians prove Mirzakhani's twist torus conjecture, showing how certain geometric objects spread evenly across the moduli space of hyperbolic surfaces.
    Why it's here: 12 weeks old; 2 citations
    source
  7. Pathos raises $237M at $3B valuation, signs Bristol Myers neuro partnership — Fierce Biotech, STAT, Endpoints News · AI for biology & medicine
    AI drug discovery company Pathos AI raised $237 million at a $3 billion valuation and struck a Bristol Myers Squibb partnership to pursue Alzheimer's treatments.
    Why it's here: 13 days old; covered by 3 outlets across 1 outlet type (biotech/health trade press)
    source · STAT · Endpoints News · Fierce Biotech
  8. Neural networks are clean — already-clean.goodfire.com · AI
    A widely discussed essay argues that neural networks' seemingly tangled neurons are more interpretable than the field assumed, reigniting debate on Hacker News.

    source · Hacker News discussion
  9. Simultaneous high-fidelity single-qubit gates in a spin qubit array — Nature Physics · Science beyond biology
    Researchers achieved gate fidelities above 99.99 percent while operating up to five silicon spin qubits simultaneously, clearing a key fault-tolerance threshold.
    Why it's here: 3 weeks old; 10 citations
    source

Transcript

Welcome to your science briefing for Thursday, November 5. Today we move across scales, from cancer clinical trials and cellular atlases to seabird navigation, pure mathematics, and quantum hardware.

We start with oncology. Roche's experimental KRAS G12C inhibitor, divarasib, beat two approved rivals head to head in a Phase 3 trial for previously treated non-small cell lung cancer with a KRAS G12C mutation. According to data Roche presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology congress, and reported by Endpoints News, Fierce Biotech, and STAT, the open-label Krascendo 1 trial enrolled 338 patients, randomized to divarasib once daily or to Amgen's Lumakras or Bristol Myers Squibb's Krazati. Median overall survival was 17.7 months with divarasib versus 12 months in the control arm, a 44 percent reduction in risk of death as reported by Endpoints News. Progression-free survival was also longer, 9.8 months versus 5.7 months, and the objective response rate was 58 percent versus 32 percent. Fierce Biotech reports that fewer patients on divarasib discontinued treatment due to side effects. This is company-presented trial data, not yet published in a peer-reviewed journal, but it's been covered by three independent biotech outlets, reflecting its significance in a field where head-to-head drug trials are rare.

Next, a biology story that traveled fast. Researchers tracked Manx shearwaters, a seabird that breeds in the British Isles, to ask whether long ocean flights could desynchronize their internal clocks, the same mechanism behind jet lag in humans. The findings, published in the journal Science and described by Science News, NPR, the Guardian, and Ars Technica, draw on two decades of GPS tracking data from more than a thousand birds, covering over 1,800 homeward flights. The authors, led by researchers including Tim Guilford and Patrick Lewin at the University of Oxford, calculated how a mismatch between a bird's internal clock and local sun time should distort its sun-based compass, then compared that prediction to actual flight paths. The birds veered off course by as much as 15 degrees, Science News reports, with NPR noting the maximum observed deviation was about 7 degrees in Lewin's account, adding only a few extra kilometers to the trip, not enough to threaten their ability to find home. Notably, the errors persisted even when birds were near familiar coastline, suggesting they weigh the sun compass against landmarks rather than simply overriding one with the other. This is a peer-reviewed paper based on real-world animal tracking, and it drew coverage across five outlets in science, general, and trade press, enough traction that we're including it a bit earlier than usual.

Staying with biology, a Nature paper from researchers at the Wellcome and Medical Research Council Cambridge Stem Cell Institute, with colleagues at the University of Cambridge, maps the developing human heart in unprecedented detail. Using single-cell and spatial multiomics, the authors defined 21 distinct tissue niches and built a classification tool called TissueTypist. They resolved three subtypes of pacemaker cells in the developing sinoatrial node and traced how heart muscle cells mature over time, including a shift in lipid metabolism. Critically, when the team compared hearts with trisomy 21, the genetic cause of Down syndrome, to typical hearts, they found fewer compact heart muscle cells and more cell death, a result they validated in stem-cell-derived heart cells matched for genetic background. The authors suggest these early developmental differences may help explain why congenital heart disease is more common in Down syndrome. This peer-reviewed study has drawn 12 citations in its first month, a solid early signal for a dataset meant to serve as a long-term resource.

From heart development to cancer genomes: a Cell paper from the University of Washington and the Brotman Baty Institute tackles a long-standing blind spot in cancer genetics. Conventional cancer genome analyses rely on a reference genome that's missing large stretches of repetitive DNA. The authors paired a near-complete, telomere-to-telomere genome assembly from a melanoma patient with deep sequencing of their tumor, and found that 16 percent of somatic mutations fall in regions absent from the standard reference genome, with satellite repeats acting as hotspots for ultraviolet-linked mutations. They also identified the DNA regions where chromosomes attach to the cell's machinery during division as frequent sites of structural variation, a pattern present in non-cancerous tissue too, while extensive epigenetic changes in those same regions appeared specific to the tumor. The paper also reconstructed cycles of telomere shortening and lengthening during tumor evolution. It's peer-reviewed, five weeks old, and has already accumulated 14 citations, reflecting interest in finally probing genomic territory cancer researchers have long had to ignore.

In computational biology, a Cell paper from the Arc Research Institute describes scBaseCount, a database built by an AI agent that automatically discovers and standardizes single-cell sequencing data mined from public archives. The authors report it's now the largest public repository of its kind, covering more than 502 million cells across 27 organisms and 75 tissues, with uniform processing that captures both coding and non-coding gene activity. They present it as a template for using AI to curate biological data at scale. This peer-reviewed paper is nine weeks old and has already drawn 41 citations, a strong signal that other researchers are finding it useful.

Switching to pure mathematics: a paper in the Duke Mathematical Journal, by researchers at the University of California, Berkeley and the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in the Sciences, resolves a conjecture posed by the late mathematician Maryam Mirzakhani about the behavior of certain geometric objects called twist tori within the moduli space of hyperbolic surfaces. The authors show that as these twist tori expand, they spread out evenly, in a precise mathematical sense, along almost all directions, while identifying other families that behave in a fundamentally different, more singular way. This kind of pure math result tends to accumulate citations slowly, with two so far after twelve weeks, but publication in a top journal is itself a strong form of vetting.

On the business side of AI and medicine, Pathos AI announced a $237 million Series E funding round led by Bristol Myers Squibb, valuing the company at roughly 3 billion dollars, according to STAT and Endpoints News. The company, which has focused on oncology, is expanding into neurological conditions, starting with Alzheimer's disease, through a new partnership with Bristol Myers Squibb and a data-sharing deal with Tempus AI. Pathos says its platform, called Foundry, runs thousands of software agents that analyze clinical, genomic, and biological data to estimate a drug candidate's probability of success before and during trials. This is a company funding announcement, not an independent evaluation of the technology's performance, and it's been covered by three trade outlets.

In artificial intelligence research, an essay from a researcher affiliated with Goodfire, previously involved in interpretability work at OpenAI and Anthropic-adjacent projects, argues that neural networks may be easier to understand than the field has assumed. The author contends that so-called polysemantic neurons, cases where a single neuron appears to respond to multiple unrelated concepts, were often misinterpreted, and reflect ordinary generalization rather than deliberate concept-packing under memory pressure. Revisiting a classic image model, the author reports that after routine architectural fixes, the vast majority of neurons became interpretable, and in preliminary audits of a modern language model, estimates that around 90 percent of neurons have one clear function. This is a self-published technical essay, not a peer-reviewed paper, so its claims haven't been independently verified, but it drew substantial attention on Hacker News, with 849 points and 344 comments, indicating real interest from the technical community in what it implies for interpreting AI systems.

Finally, in quantum computing, a paper in Nature Physics from researchers at National Taiwan University and RIKEN in Japan reports progress on a persistent engineering problem: running high-fidelity operations on multiple qubits at once. Working with a five-qubit silicon spin array, the authors identified microwave-induced frequency shifts as the main cause of errors during simultaneous operation, and introduced a calibration method to correct for it. They report individual qubit gate fidelities above 99.99 percent, with some reaching 99.999 percent, and fidelities staying above 99.99 percent when operating three qubits at once. Even with all five qubits running in parallel, fidelities stayed above 99.9 percent, the commonly cited threshold for fault-tolerant quantum computing. This peer-reviewed paper is three weeks old and has drawn 10 citations, an encouraging signal for a hardware approach that depends on industrial chip manufacturing techniques.

That's today's briefing. Thanks for listening, and we'll be back tomorrow with more.

Transcript

Welcome to your science briefing for Wednesday, November 4. Today we cover a lung cancer trial result, advances in brain organoids and bat genomics, a new genomic language model, a proof in pure mathematics, AI-driven drug screening, a security story about Claude Code extensions, a fast radio burst from early in the universe's history, and a critical essay on Anthropic's ambitions in biology.

First, oncology. According to Endpoints News, Amgen's drug Imdelltra, combined with AstraZeneca's Imfinzi, cut the risk of death by 58 percent compared to Imfinzi alone, in a phase 3 trial testing the combination as first-line maintenance therapy for certain small-cell lung cancer patients. Endpoints reports the combination added eight months of life, with the results presented at the ESMO oncology conference. This is a single trade press report, so independent confirmation and the full trial data are still to come, but a survival benefit of this size in small-cell lung cancer would be clinically significant. The story made our list because it's a concrete, large-magnitude result from a major cancer conference, even though so far only one outlet has covered it.

Next, two papers on longevity biology. The first, published in Nature, comes from researchers at the Broad Institute, Harvard University, and the University of Milan. The authors grew human brain organoids, which are lab-grown clusters of brain tissue, for an unprecedented five years in culture. They report that these organoids continue to transcriptionally and epigenetically age in ways that track real time, with the organoids' predicted biological age correlating closely with how long they'd spent in the dish. In a clever experiment, the team mixed young and old neural progenitor cells together and found the old cells rapidly produced late-stage neurons, skipping earlier developmental stages, while young cells in the same dish followed the normal sequence. The authors conclude that these cells retain a kind of internal memory of elapsed time. This paper has drawn 26 citations in about 11 weeks, and it matters because studying the multi-year arc of human brain development has been nearly impossible in animal models.

The second longevity paper, also in Nature, comes from Pennsylvania State University and the University of California, Berkeley. Researchers sequenced genomes from eight closely related Myotis bat species, animals known for unusually long lifespans and resistance to disease. The authors report distinct patterns of genetic adaptation for fighting DNA viruses versus RNA viruses, and they identify multiple ancient duplicated copies of an immune gene called PKR that have persisted across species for a long time. They also link bats' longevity to positive selection in cancer-related pathways and observed a distinct DNA damage response in cells from one especially long-lived species, Myotis lucifugus. This study has 16 citations after 10 weeks and offers a genetic basis for the long-standing puzzle of why bats age slowly and tolerate viruses so well.

Moving to computational biology, a team from UC Berkeley and the Innovative Genomics Institute published a new genomic language model in Nature called GPN-Star. Unlike many AI models borrowed from natural language processing, this one is built with an architecture that explicitly accounts for evolutionary relationships, using whole-genome alignments and species trees. The authors report it achieves state-of-the-art performance predicting the effects of genetic variants, both in protein-coding and non-coding regions, and that it substantially outperforms previous methods at flagging disease-causing variants identified in genome-wide association studies. They also extended the approach to five other organisms, including mice, fruit flies, and a flowering plant, to test its generalizability. The paper has 22 citations in eight weeks, and it's noteworthy as a solid methods advance in a field crowded with AI hype, specifically that smarter model design can beat sheer scale.

In pure mathematics, a paper now published in the Journal of the American Mathematical Society, by Morris Ang and colleagues, settles a long-conjectured formula connecting two areas of probability theory and mathematical physics. The authors prove a prediction, originally made in 2010, about the exact probabilities governing how points cluster together in two-dimensional critical percolation, a model used to study phenomena like the spread of fluids through random media. Their proof relies on a connection between conformal loop ensembles, which describe random curves, and Liouville quantum gravity, a mathematical framework from string theory. They also resolve a related 2015 conjecture about nesting statistics of these loop structures. The paper has already picked up 26 citations in 12 weeks, fast recognition for a pure math result, reflecting how it ties together several previously separate strands of conjecture.

Now, AI applied to drug discovery. Researchers from the University of Pavia, St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, and Harvard University, writing in Nature Biotechnology, introduce an open-source platform called AdaptiveFlow for screening enormous virtual chemical libraries. The authors report it provides free access to a screening-ready version of a commercial library containing 69 billion compounds, and that a new method for organizing molecular properties cuts computational costs by roughly a thousandfold. An optional active-learning component can further steer the search toward molecules likely to bind a chosen target. The authors say the platform scaled across up to 5.6 million cloud computing processors, and they used it to find nanomolar-strength inhibitors for two disease-relevant proteins, validating the hits experimentally and solving new crystal structures showing how the inhibitors bind. This paper has drawn 27 citations in nine weeks, reflecting real traction for a tool addressing a persistent bottleneck in finding new drug candidates.

From the Hacker News community, a fast-moving story this week concerns backdoors discovered in official extensions for Claude Code, Anthropic's AI coding assistant. The post, from the account cyberplace dot social, drew 662 points and 17 comments on Hacker News in just five days. Only the headline is available in the material we have, so we can't detail the mechanism or scope of the backdoors here, but the scale of attention, hundreds of points within days, signals this is a story worth watching for further reporting on what exactly was compromised and how.

In astrophysics, a team led by researchers at the University of Sydney, publishing in Science, report detecting a fast radio burst, a millisecond-duration radio flash from outside our galaxy, originating from a galaxy at redshift 2.148. That corresponds to roughly three billion years after the Big Bang, making it one of the most distant such bursts identified with a confirmed host galaxy. The authors say the host is a small, clumpy, star-forming galaxy, and the burst occurred during the period when star formation across the universe was at its peak. They note the burst's radio signal was heavily scattered, suggesting there's a whole population of similarly distant fast radio bursts that current surveys are missing. The paper has nine citations after four weeks and extends the distance over which these mysterious transients can be used to probe the structure of intergalactic gas.

A daily science briefing covering new virology and genome-editing tools, Nvidia and the University of Washington's open protein-design model, Anthropic's drug-discovery ambitions, a CAR-T safety signal at Bristol Myers Squibb, and this year's Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

  1. Aminopeptidase N is a receptor for hedgehog merbecoviruses — Nature Microbiology · Biology & biomedical research
    Researchers identified aminopeptidase N as the cell-entry receptor for hedgehog-dwelling merbecoviruses related to MERS, mapping a distinct spike-receptor interface via cryo-electron microscopy.
    Why it's here: 7 weeks old; 12 citations
    source
  2. Nature's capacity to 'bounce back' when species are lost is overestimated: study — phys.org · Biology & biomedical research
    A widely discussed phys.org headline reports a study finding that ecosystems' ability to recover after species loss has been overestimated.
    Why it's here: 4 weeks old; 355 Hacker News points / 181 comments

  3. Virus-like particles enable targeted gene engineering and pooled CRISPR screening in primary human myeloid cells — Nature Biotechnology · Computational biology & bioinformatics
    A new virus-like particle toolkit enables efficient CRISPR editing and pooled genetic screening in primary human myeloid cells, revealing TNFAIP3 as a key regulator of inflammatory polarization.
    Why it's here: 11 weeks old; 5 citations
    source
  4. Navier–Stokes Lost in Translation — arxiv.org · Mathematics
    A preprint argues that Lean-verifying an AI-translated proof, including OpenAI's announced Navier-Stokes blow-up proof, does not guarantee the original natural-language argument was correct.
    Why it's here: 4 weeks old; 361 Hacker News points / 240 comments
    source · Hacker News discussion
  5. Anthropic's biopharma research update highlights AI's role in drug discovery — Endpoints News, The Verge (AI), Fierce Biotech · AI for biology & medicine
    Anthropic's IPO filing details its expansion into drug discovery, including its own lab and a biotech acquisition, while separate reporting highlights the company's reliance on natural gas-powered data centers.
    Why it's here: 8 days old; covered by 3 outlets across 2 outlet types (biotech/health trade press, tech press); 1728 Hacker News points / 440 comments; fast-tracked: younger than the usual waiting period, admitted on exceptional traction
    source · Hacker News discussion · The Verge (AI) · Fierce Biotech · Endpoints News
  6. Nvidia, UW Institute for Protein Design unveil open-source protein design AI model — GEN · AI for biology & medicine
    Nvidia and the University of Washington's Institute for Protein Design released RFD4-Proteina, an open-source generative model the developers say speeds up and improves success rates for designing new proteins.
    Why it's here: 12 days old; covered by 1 outlet across 1 outlet type (biotech/health trade press)
    source
  7. DeepSeek banned from U.S. federal civilian agencies under new DHS order — reuters.com · AI

    Why it's here: 15 days old; 584 Hacker News points / 544 comments

  8. BMS CAR-T trial reveals patient death; company reports safety signal in lupus program — Endpoints News, STAT · Biotech & pharma
    Bristol Myers Squibb disclosed a patient death in an early-stage autoimmune CAR-T trial for multiple sclerosis, adding to safety concerns in the field, according to STAT and Endpoints News.
