Transcript

Welcome to your science and biotech briefing for Monday, October 19. Today we cover a major autoimmune acquisition, a pharma industry lawsuit over drug pricing, striking findings on coral and tortoise biology, an AI system that found new biology on its own, a frontier math result, a big AI-for-biology funding push, a new AI model release, and a catalyst-free way to break down plastic.

First, dealmaking. Fierce Biotech reports that Novartis is acquiring an asset from the China-based company Abogen Biosciences for 575 million dollars upfront, with up to 7.2 billion dollars more in potential milestones, bringing the deal's total value to about 7.8 billion dollars. The asset, called ABO2203, is a messenger RNA, or mRNA, encoded T-cell engager meant to treat autoimmune disease. Instead of manufacturing the drug in a factory, the mRNA is injected and directs the patient's own cells to produce the engager, which depletes the B cells thought to drive autoimmune conditions. According to Fierce Biotech, Abogen's partner Ruijin Hospital has run early trials, and published data showed the drug depleted B cells in three patients with the blood disorder immune thrombocytopenia, without causing the cytokine release syndrome that can complicate similar therapies. This comes weeks after Novartis paused a separate autoimmune CAR-T program following three deaths, so the outlet frames this deal as the company recalibrating its approach to B-cell depletion rather than retreating from it. It's worth flagging this is one outlet's reporting, built substantially on the companies' own announcement, so the early clinical claims should be read as promising but preliminary.

Next, a policy fight. STAT and Endpoints News both report that the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America, the main trade group for brand-name drugmakers, is suing the Trump administration over a Medicare pilot program called GLOBE. The program ties Medicare Part B drug prices to prices paid in peer countries, using a so-called most-favored-nation approach. According to STAT, PhRMA's complaint, filed in federal court in Washington, argues the pilot exceeds Medicare's statutory authority. STAT also notes the program's practical impact may be limited, since the administration exempted all but a handful of companies in exchange for voluntary deals to charge Medicaid the most-favored-nation prices. Still, this is a real legal clash between the industry and the government over how far the executive branch can go in reshaping drug pricing, and it's being tracked by two of the major biotech trade outlets.

Now to biology. Nature and Science both report on a coral study published in the journal Science Advances. Researchers at Hopkins Marine Station, led by Stephen Palumbi with Danny Collins as a key investigator, noticed that two fragments of the coral species Pocillopora damicornis, one bleached and one healthy, had accidentally come into contact in a lab tank, and color appeared to be seeping into the bleached piece. They followed up with a controlled experiment: ten pairs of bleached and healthy fragments from the same coral individual, five pairs touching, five separated by a few millimeters. According to Nature, the touching pairs fully recovered within eight weeks, with the population of symbiotic algae doubling roughly every four days by the second week, far faster than coral recovery rates seen in the wild. After just one week of contact, a bleached fragment could continue recovering even once separated. The non-touching pairs, by contrast, died by twenty weeks. Using high-powered microscopy, the team found the fragments were fusing via a tissue bridge that let algae transfer across, but this only worked between fragments from the same genetic individual, not between different corals or species. The authors describe this as grounds for hope about reef recovery strategies, though the work was done in a lab setting with one coral species, and scaling it to reef conservation remains an open question.

Staying with biology, several outlets, including the Guardian, GEN, and the New York Times, covered a study on Jonathan, a giant tortoise living in Saint Helena believed to be 194 years old. A team led by Stephen Clark at the nonprofit Kallel Foundation sequenced Jonathan's genome and methylome, the pattern of chemical tags that silence genes, and compared it with those of four younger tortoises of the same species. According to GEN, the researchers identified 287 gene variants that may reduce typical aging effects. The more notable finding, reported by the Guardian, was that while most of Jonathan's gene-silencing patterns looked like those of other old tortoises, the patterns on genes tied to mitochondrial function, the structures that power cells, closely resembled those of much younger animals. The study, published in Science Advances, concludes that keeping these gene-regulation patterns stable is linked to efficient energy production and DNA repair. The researchers are careful to note it's unclear whether or how much this contributes to Jonathan's long life, and Clark said the next step is testing whether manipulating mitochondria can actually extend lifespan. This is one animal, not a controlled experiment, so it's descriptive and suggestive rather than causal evidence.

Turning to computational biology, Nature, BBC Science, and Wired all picked up on Anthropic's announcement that its AI model Claude identified an enzyme system in viral genomes that the company says has features reminiscent of CRISPR, the gene-editing tool. According to Wired, Anthropic ran about 950 Claude agents simultaneously, which sifted through more than 200,000 candidate reverse transcriptases, proteins that copy RNA into DNA, narrowing down to an unusual family found in large bacteria-infecting viruses called jumbo phages. Anthropic calls the system ART, for array-associated reverse transcriptases. The company itself says, quote, we don't yet understand what this system does, end quote, and the finding comes from a technical report that has not been peer-reviewed, with only one physical lab experiment included so far. Outside scientists quoted by Wired, including Stanford's Le Cong, are skeptical of the hype, with Cong noting that finding something interesting computationally is only the first step toward knowing if it's actually useful. Nature also reports that a University of Copenhagen scientist studying related microbial systems said he'd previously uploaded relevant information to Anthropic's models, raising questions about how novel the discovery really is. So, an intriguing computational lead, not yet a validated finding.

On now to a few shorter items. In pure mathematics, the journal Inventiones Mathematicae published a paper by Wangjian Jian and colleagues from the Chinese Academy of Sciences, the Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, and Peking University, on finite-time singularities of the Kähler-Ricci flow, a tool in geometric analysis for understanding how curved shapes evolve over time. The paper is brand new, with no citations yet, but it appears in one of the field's top venues, which is itself a meaningful form of vetting for a slow-moving area of math. Beyond that, limited material is available on its specific findings.

In AI for biology, Biohub, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the National Institutes of Health announced what they describe as the largest coordinated commitment yet to generating what they call AI-ready biological data, totaling 1.8 billion dollars in funding, data, computation, and new measurement technology. According to the announcement, the Department of Energy will contribute more than 500 million dollars over five years, the NIH will coordinate existing biomedical datasets, and Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs, and Meta are jointly putting in 300 million dollars toward what's called the Virtual Biology Initiative. The stated goal is to build predictive AI models of cells that let researchers run experiments digitally. This is a press release from the organizations involved, so treat the framing as their own characterization, but the story drew 150 points on Hacker News, suggesting strong interest in the AI-and-biology community.

In general AI news, the company x.ai released Grok 4.7, which it describes as its most capable model yet for coding and knowledge work. According to the company's own announcement, the model uses a larger base architecture than its predecessor, was trained with a longer reinforcement-learning run on harder tasks, and is built with a new safety stack the company says performs well on refusal and jailbreak-resistance tests, including a reported 62.4 percent score on a biosafety benchmark from LatchBio. This is entirely a company announcement, with all benchmark figures coming from x.ai itself, but it drew over 600 points and 540 comments on Hacker News, indicating substantial developer interest.

Finally, in chemistry, a paper in Nature from Ruiliang Gao and colleagues at Zhejiang University's State Key Laboratory of Clean Energy Utilization describes a catalyst-free method for breaking down waste plastic into carboxylic acids, using hydroxyl radicals generated at microdroplet interfaces. The authors report complete conversion of polyethylene, with selectivity toward short-chain diacids approaching 69 percent under mild conditions, and say the method scaled successfully up to 300 grams in testing. The paper has picked up five citations since publication in July, a modest but real signal of early attention in a field where catalyst poisoning and cost have been long-standing obstacles to plastic upcycling.

That's the briefing for today. Thanks for listening, and we'll be back tomorrow with more.

A rundown of full Phase 3 data on Lilly's retatrutide and GLP-1 aging-clock findings, a provocative AI-claimed lab discovery and OpenAI's new agent product, plus notable advances in pangenome variant cataloging, polaron mathematics, acidic water electrolysis catalysts, and a deep look at the reliability of AI-assisted formal math.

  1. Lilly's retatrutide shows full Phase 3 data for obesity, positioning as next-generation GLP-1/GIP/GCG therapy — Fierce Biotech · Biotech & pharma
    Fierce Biotech details full Phase 3 data showing Lilly's retatrutide drove over 20% average weight loss at the top dose, positioning it ahead of existing GLP-1 drugs ahead of a planned FDA filing.
    Why it's here: 18 days old; covered by 1 outlet across 1 outlet type (biotech/health trade press)
    source
  2. GLP-1 drugs show signs of slowing biological aging in humans — MIT Technology Review · Biology & biomedical research
    MIT Technology Review reports Lilly and Novo Nordisk both found reduced biological age in patients on their GLP-1 drugs using molecular aging clocks, though researchers caution the evidence doesn't yet extend to healthy people.
    Why it's here: 12 days old; covered by 1 outlet across 1 outlet type (tech press); 20 Hacker News points / 10 comments
    source
  3. Loss of cell identity drives human aging: Two new papers — erictopol.substack.com · Biology & biomedical research
    A widely discussed newsletter post flags two new papers on loss of cell identity as a driver of aging, though only the headline was available for this summary.
    Why it's here: 17 days old; 375 Hacker News points / 196 comments
    source · Hacker News discussion
  4. Defining and cataloging variants in pangenome graphs — Cell Genomics · Computational biology & bioinformatics
    Broad Institute and Harvard researchers introduce a new method for defining genetic variants in pangenome graphs, cataloging nearly 30 million variants including millions invisible to standard reference genomes.
    Why it's here: 9 weeks old; 4 citations
    source
  5. OpenAI claims Claude made autonomous scientific discovery in laboratory setting — New York Times, Endpoints News · AI for biology & medicine
    Anthropic says its Claude AI autonomously discovered a new enzyme system, though a University of Copenhagen researcher noted the finding matched work his team had already shared with the model.
    Why it's here: 20 days old; covered by 2 outlets across 2 outlet types (general press, biotech/health trade press); 13 Hacker News points / 4 comments
    source · Endpoints News
  6. OpenAI introduces Dots, always-on AI agents competing with Meta's Muse — The Verge (AI), Wired (AI) · AI
    OpenAI launched Dots, always-on AI agents that work across thousands of connected apps, directly challenging Meta's popular Muse assistant.
    Why it's here: 19 days old; covered by 2 outlets across 1 outlet type (tech press)
    source · Wired (AI)
  7. Proof of the Landau-Pekar formula for the effective mass of the polaron at strong coupling — Inventiones mathematicae · Mathematics

    Why it's here: 12 weeks old; 1 citations
    source
  8. Octahedral-coordinated Co3O4 for water electrolysis in acid — Nature · Science beyond biology
    A proof published in Inventiones Mathematicae confirms the 1987 Landau-Pekar conjecture on the effective mass of the strongly coupled polaron.

    source
  9. What mathematicians should know about the Lean Theorem Prover: questions of reliability and AI — What's New (Terence Tao) · Worth reading

    Why it's here: 9 days old; 208 Hacker News points / 58 comments
    source

Transcript

Welcome to your science briefing for Sunday, October 18. Today we cover new obesity drug data, questions about whether weight-loss drugs slow aging, a disputed claim of AI-driven lab discovery, a new always-on AI agent, and notable results in genomics, mathematics, and materials chemistry.

We start with biotech and pharma. Fierce Biotech reports that Eli Lilly has released detailed Phase 3 data for its triple-agonist drug retatrutide, which acts on the GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptors. The trial, called Triumph-2, enrolled 1,152 adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes. On the top, 12 milligram dose, average weight loss was 20.8% at week 80, compared with a 4% drop on placebo. More than a third of patients on that dose lost at least a quarter of their body weight, and over half lost at least a fifth. Lilly also reported improvements in several cardiovascular risk markers, including triglycerides, cholesterol, blood pressure, and a marker of inflammation called C-reactive protein. The outlet notes the drug had a more modest effect on blood sugar control than Lilly's existing drug tirzepatide, with fewer patients reaching healthy blood sugar levels. Lilly, according to Fierce Biotech, plans to file for FDA approval in the first quarter of next year. This is company-reported trial data, published alongside a presentation in The Lancet, so it carries more weight than a press release alone, though it comes from the manufacturer itself. It made today's list because it's the first full dataset behind a widely anticipated obesity drug, and because rival companies are already racing to match or beat these results.

Staying with GLP-1 drugs, MIT Technology Review reports that Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk both say patients on their weight-loss drugs show signs of slower biological aging, based on so-called molecular aging clocks that estimate biological age from DNA changes or blood protein levels. According to the article, Novo measured blood from just over ten thousand people, half on semaglutide and half on placebo, and found reductions in estimated biological age of roughly two to three years, varying by clock type and tissue measured. Lilly ran a smaller study using tirzepatide and reported similar, if less dramatic, results using DNA-based clocks. These findings were presented at a conference on aging research, not yet published as peer-reviewed papers, so they should be read as company-reported readouts. Scientists quoted in the piece, including aging-clock pioneer Steve Horvath, called the effect notable but cautioned that it's unclear whether these drugs would benefit people who aren't overweight, partly because of side effects like muscle loss. A federally funded study is now underway to test anti-aging effects in healthy older adults. This item made the cut because it generated substantial discussion online and connects two major pharmaceutical storylines to aging biology more broadly.

Next, a story we can only sketch briefly. A piece from Eric Topol's newsletter, titled "Loss of cell identity drives human aging," discusses two new papers on that topic. Our source material for this item was limited to the headline, so we can't describe the papers' methods or findings here. It's worth flagging only because it drew a large amount of discussion on Hacker News, suggesting real interest in this area of aging biology, but listeners should look to the original papers for substance.

Moving to computational biology, a paper in Cell Genomics from researchers at the Broad Institute, Harvard, and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute tackles a technical problem in genomics: how to define genetic variants when using pangenome graphs instead of a single reference genome. Comparing a person's DNA to just one reference sequence, like the standard human genome, can introduce errors, especially in regions with complex structural differences. The authors introduce a method called pantree that organizes multiple reference genomes into a tree structure to identify variants more consistently. Applying this to an existing draft pangenome graph, they catalogued 29.6 million genetic variants. Most were small, and most of those were single-letter changes. Notably, about 3.5 million variants had a reference version of the sequence that isn't even present in the standard human genome, meaning these variants would be nearly invisible to conventional analysis. The authors highlight two medically relevant regions, the HLA-A and RHD genes, where they found thousands of small variants embedded in complicated structural rearrangements. This is a peer-reviewed methods paper, and it made our list because it's accumulating citations faster than typical for its age, suggesting other researchers are already finding the tool useful.

Now to artificial intelligence and biology, a story worth some skepticism. The New York Times and Endpoints News report that Anthropic says its AI system, Claude, made what the company calls its first autonomous scientific discovery, identifying a new enzyme system in a laboratory setting. According to the coverage, a researcher at the University of Copenhagen said his team had been sharing their own research with Claude, and that the AI's reported finding matched work they were already doing. This detail raises real questions about how independent the discovery actually was. Our source material here is thin, built mainly from company statements and brief press coverage, so we should treat the word discovery cautiously, since it comes primarily from the company itself. This item made the list because it's covered by both general and biotech trade press and sparked real debate online about what counts as an AI making a scientific finding versus confirming existing human research.

Still on AI, The Verge and Wired both covered OpenAI's launch of a new product called Dots, announced at the company's developer conference. Dots are described as always-on AI assistants that run in the background across more than four thousand connected apps, using a cloud computer to browse the web and complete multistep tasks while learning a user's preferences over time. They're OpenAI's answer to Meta's Muse, a similar assistant that reportedly became hugely popular but also drew safety concerns, including one reported incident where Muse shared a user's address without permission during a marketplace transaction. OpenAI says Dots include built-in rules about when to act independently versus asking for permission, plus a review feature meant to check actions against safety requirements. The rollout starts with OpenAI's higher-priced subscription tiers. This is straightforward company product coverage, confirmed by two independent tech outlets, and it matters because it signals the agentic AI assistant space is now a genuine two-way contest between major tech companies.

Switching to mathematics. A paper in Inventiones Mathematicae by Morris Brooks proves a seventy-plus-year-old conjecture about the Fröhlich polaron, a theoretical model describing how an electron interacts with vibrations in a crystal. The paper establishes a precise lower bound on the polaron's effective mass under strong coupling conditions, and combined with an earlier upper bound proven by the author with Robert Seiringer, this confirms what's called the Landau-Pekar formula, a prediction made in 1948 and formally conjectured by Herbert Spohn in 1987. This is a peer-reviewed proof in one of the field's top journals, and in mathematics, publication there functions as its own form of vetting, even with just one citation so far given how slowly this subfield moves.

In materials science, a paper in Nature from researchers at Xiamen University and Soochow University describes a new catalyst for splitting water in acidic conditions, a key step for producing hydrogen fuel. Current approaches often rely on iridium, a rare and expensive metal. The authors created a new crystal structure of cobalt oxide, arranged so that cobalt atoms sit in a highly active coordination pattern throughout the material rather than mixed with less active sites, which limits conventional cobalt oxide catalysts. They report this material needs substantially less voltage to drive the reaction at a standard test current than ordinary cobalt oxide, and that it can sustain high current density in a working electrolysis device. The authors say the structure helps the material resist breaking down, a key stability metric for industrial use. This peer-reviewed paper has drawn notably more citations than typical for its age, suggesting strong interest from the catalysis community.

Finally, worth reading: a guest post on mathematician Terence Tao's blog, written by Thomas Hales, examines the reliability of the Lean theorem prover, a software system mathematicians use to formally verify proofs at the level of basic logic. Hales walks through recent milestones in what's called autoformalization, where AI systems translate existing mathematical papers into formal, machine-checkable proofs, including large projects this year covering Fermat's Last Theorem and a Navier-Stokes blowup result. He then explains the underlying type theory Lean is built on and stresses that any Lean proof depends entirely on the correctness of Lean's small verification kernel, cautioning that such proofs shouldn't be trusted until properly checked. This is an expert's own analysis rather than a peer-reviewed study, but it drew a large amount of discussion online, reflecting how unsettled questions about AI and mathematical certainty have become this year.

That's today's briefing. Thanks for listening, and we'll be back tomorrow with more.

    source · Hugging Face
  7. OpenAI GPT–6 Astra breaks Enigma message that has resisted solution since 2005 — cryptocellar.org · AI
    OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra reportedly broke a 1941 Enigma-encrypted message unsolved since 2005 by independently building its own code-breaking tools, according to a widely discussed cryptography blog post.

    source · Hacker News discussion
  8. New Nuclear Clocks Tick at Lutetium Atoms for Record Precision — Nature, New York Times · Science beyond biology

Transcript

Welcome to your Saturday, October 17 science briefing. Today we trace how artificial intelligence is showing up across mathematics, medicine, and cryptography, alongside notable findings in genetics and physics. Let's start with biotech. Fierce Biotech, BioPharma Dive, and Endpoints News all covered early trial results from Adicet Bio for its cell therapy, prula-cel, in lupus. This is a company announcement describing a small, early-stage human trial, not yet peer-reviewed. According to Fierce Biotech, after one year of follow-up, twelve of twenty-two evaluated patients achieved remission of lupus symptoms, and eight of sixteen patients with kidney involvement, called lupus nephritis, saw their kidney symptoms go into remission. BioPharma Dive reports slightly different framing: half of evaluable lupus nephritis patients had a complete kidney response, and fifty-four percent met a standard statistical definition of remission. All of these patients had failed multiple prior therapies, and all stopped using immunosuppressive drugs. Unlike other CAR-T approaches that use a patient's own modified T cells, prula-cel is made from donor-derived gamma delta T cells, an off-the-shelf approach the company says may cause fewer severe side effects. Notably, there were no serious cases of a dangerous inflammatory syndrome that recently led to deaths in a Novartis autoimmune trial using a different CAR-T design. BioPharma Dive also notes that about a quarter of patients had mild to moderate cytokine release syndrome, and infections occurred in more than half of patients, with some severe. Despite the data, Adicet's stock dropped twenty-two percent on the day, according to BioPharma Dive. This story made the cut because it's been covered by three biotech trade outlets over the past nineteen days, and represents an early but closely watched milestone in applying cell therapy to autoimmune disease. Next, a major genetics paper. Nature Medicine published a genome-wide association study meta-analysis on fibromyalgia, led by Isabel Kerrebijn and colleagues at Mount Sinai Hospital and the University of Toronto. This is a peer-reviewed paper analyzing genetic data from more than two and a half million people, including about fifty-five thousand fibromyalgia cases, pooled across eleven cohorts. The authors identified twenty-six genetic risk regions for fibromyalgia. The strongest signal was a coding variant in the gene HTT, the same gene responsible for Huntington's disease. Other implicated genes have roles in the nervous system. The authors report that fibromyalgia's heritability is concentrated specifically in brain tissues and neural cell types, and that the condition shares strong genetic overlap with other chronic pain and psychiatric conditions, including low back pain, post-traumatic stress disorder, and irritable bowel syndrome, with genetic correlations above zero point seven for each. Despite large differences in how often fibromyalgia is diagnosed in men versus women, the authors found the underlying genetic architecture was nearly identical between sexes. This paper has drawn eight citations in the twelve weeks since publication, and it's a substantial step toward treating fibromyalgia as a disorder rooted in the central nervous system rather than a vaguely defined syndrome. Two shorter items from Nature's news pages touch on cancer genomics and genome mapping, though the available material is limited. Nature reported on research into extrachromosomal circular DNA, a form of DNA that exists outside the normal chromosomes in some cancer cells and is known to drive tumor evolution. The available text was mostly a reference list rather than a full article, so we can't detail specific findings here, but the piece points to structural fragility in this circular DNA as a potential vulnerability researchers are studying in cancer cells. Separately, Nature also covered new work mapping which parts of the genome are physically accessible for gene activity, a technique that can reveal disease risk signals not visible through gene expression studies alone. Again, the detailed findings weren't available in the material provided, so we'll flag this as a topic to watch rather than summarize specifics. Now to mathematics and artificial intelligence, where today's through-line really comes together. A blog post on the site overreacted-dot-io, which drew two hundred seventy-one points and nearly three hundred comments on Hacker News, describes an attempt to get a frontier AI model to help prove a decades-old open conjecture in mathematics. The author, with no claimed mathematical expertise, asked the AI assistant Claude to pick an unsolved problem in the theory of surreal numbers, John Conway's number system that contains every real number, every infinite ordinal, and combinations of both. Claude selected what it described as Conway's last remaining conjecture about his own invention, posed in 1976: that if a times b equals c times d among a certain class of numbers called omnific integers, then all four numbers can be broken into shared building blocks. Working with the model over roughly a month, the author produced a proof formalized in the Lean theorem-proving language. The author is explicit that this proof has not been independently verified by professional mathematicians, though it has passed automated mechanical checks in a registry called Palomar, and some people familiar with both Lean and the field say the underlying statement looks correct. The author invites mathematicians to find a flaw. This item made the cut because of the scale of community engagement around a genuinely unusual question: whether a non-mathematician guided by AI can produce a checkable proof of a known open problem. Turning to AI applied to medicine, a preprint posted to arXiv and highlighted on Hugging Face's daily papers list describes a new training method called One-stage Policy Optimization, from authors including Junying Chen. This has not been peer-reviewed. The authors say their method solves two specific failure patterns they identify in training medical language models purely through reinforcement learning, without an initial supervised fine-tuning step. Using this method, their model scored sixty-seven point two on a benchmark called HealthBench using only twenty thousand training examples, which the authors say outperformed both a standard combined training pipeline and plain reinforcement learning by several points. Scaled up into a twenty-seven billion parameter model called HuatuoGPT-3, the authors report a score of seventy point one on the overall benchmark and seventy-one point four on a professional-level subset, which they say surpasses a frontier model called GPT-6 Astra on this test. These are the authors' own benchmark numbers from a preprint, not independent verification. The paper has attracted forty-seven upvotes on Hugging Face in under two weeks, a sign of interest from the machine learning community in this training approach for domain-specific AI. Speaking of GPT-6 Astra: a report on the cryptography site cryptocellar-dot-org, which drew seven hundred thirty-eight points and more than four hundred comments on Hacker News, describes how that OpenAI model was used to break a German Army Enigma-encrypted message from July 10th, 1941, that had resisted decryption since 2005. According to the site's author, a researcher named Carter Leffen simply directed the model to attempt any unbroken Enigma message from a public archive. The model identified the most promising candidate message on its own, suspected it was related in content to an already-broken message from the same day, built its own Enigma simulator and code-breaking software, and used a repeated place name as a guessable clue to recover the correct settings and decode the message. The site's author, an experienced cryptanalyst, says the model appeared to independently locate and reference German archival records relevant to the message's origin, and that the work took the model about two days, compared to what the author estimates would take a human researcher weeks or months. This is a single documented case study from the researcher's own website, not an independently replicated study, but it drew enormous Hacker News attention as a vivid demonstration of applying large language models to a well-defined historical puzzle. In physics, Nature and the New York Times both reported on new nuclear clocks built using lutetium atoms, under the headline "Nuclear clocks tick for the first time." Nuclear clocks measure time using transitions within an atomic nucleus rather than its surrounding electrons, and physicists have pursued them for years as a path to even greater timekeeping precision than today's best atomic clocks. The detailed material available to us was limited to headlines and reference lists rather than the full reporting, so we can't give you the specific precision figures or methods here, but the story is notable simply for appearing in both a specialist science outlet and a general-interest newspaper within the same week. Finally, under today's worth-reading pick: Terence Tao, the Fields Medal-winning mathematician, published an essay titled "Math 2.0." It drew five hundred sixty-three points and five hundred fifty comments on Hacker News, enough traction that we're flagging it before our usual review period, though only the headline was available to us, so we can't summarize its arguments. Given Tao's standing and the scale of discussion, it's worth seeking out directly if you follow how AI might reshape mathematical research. That's your briefing for today. Thanks for listening, and we'll be back tomorrow.

A look at how careful vetting — peer review, archival re-analysis, and independent testing — separates durable findings from hype this week, spanning a function-field proof, a fast-adopted spatial transcriptomics tool, a DNA-history correction, a heart-valve trial, and claims about AI models in math and coding.

  1. On the generalized Ramanujan and Arthur conjectures over function fields — Annals of Mathematics · Mathematics
    A proof published in the Annals of Mathematics resolves a case of the generalized Ramanujan and Arthur conjectures over function fields using Galois parametrization and Frobenius weight theory.

  2. ResolVI: addressing noise and bias in spatial transcriptomics — Nature Methods · Computational biology & bioinformatics

  3. How did Rosalind Franklin miss the helix in her iconic DNA image? She didn't — Science (news), NPR · Biology & biomedical research
    Science news and NPR cover a new archival analysis that refutes James Watson's long-standing claim to have been first to recognize the significance of Rosalind Franklin's Photograph 51.
    Why it's here: 11 days old; covered by 2 outlets across 2 outlet types (science press, general press); 294 Hacker News points / 108 comments
    source · Hacker News discussion · NPR Science
  4. Strong evidence that 'baryon junctions' give proton its identity — Nature · Biology & biomedical research
    Reporting in Nature describes the STAR Collaboration's experimental evidence, published in Science, that baryon number is carried by structures called baryon junctions rather than by quarks themselves.
    Why it's here: 11 days old; covered by 1 outlet across 1 outlet type (science press); 3 Hacker News points / 1 comments
    source
  5. Tricuspid-Valve Intervention in Heart Failure — New England Journal of Medicine · Biotech & pharma
    A 360-patient randomized trial in the New England Journal of Medicine found transcatheter tricuspid valve repair plus medical therapy outperformed medical therapy alone on both one-year and three-year composite outcomes.
    Why it's here: 7 weeks old; 9 citations
    source
  6. Reliability of AI Methods in Drug Discovery: Evaluation of Boltz-2 for Structure and Binding Affinity Prediction — Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation · AI for biology & medicine
    An independent peer-reviewed evaluation finds the AI model Boltz-2 shows weak correlation with physics-based binding calculations and lacks the precision needed for drug lead identification.
    Why it's here: 11 weeks old; 4 citations
    source
  7. Why isn't the industry freaking out about DeepSeek 4.1 Flash? — dgt.is · AI
    A widely discussed but subjective blog post argues the open-weight model DeepSeek 4.1 Flash matches frontier AI models at a fraction of the cost, sparking debate about shifting AI economics.
    Why it's here: 8 days old; 1137 Hacker News points / 989 comments; fast-tracked: younger than the usual waiting period, admitted on exceptional traction
    source · Hacker News discussion
  8. What should we tell our students? — What's New (Terence Tao) · Worth reading
    A guest essay on Terence Tao's blog addresses anxious math students, arguing no one can yet say with confidence whether AI will surpass human mathematical research.
    Why it's here: 8 days old; 161 Hacker News points / 252 comments
    source

Transcript

Welcome to your science briefing for Friday, October 16. Today we look at how vetting — peer review, archival digging, and independent testing — separates solid progress from hype, across mathematics, biology, physics, cardiology, and artificial intelligence.

We start in mathematics. In the Annals of Mathematics, Dan Ciubotaru and colleagues at the University of Oxford and Columbia University published a proof addressing a case of the generalized Ramanujan and Arthur conjectures over function fields. In plain terms, these conjectures concern how certain building blocks of number theory, called automorphic representations, behave at different points, or places, of a mathematical field. The authors show that if such a representation behaves in a specific controlled way, called tempered, at two places, then it must behave that way at all other unramified places too. Their proof leans on a Galois parametrization method developed by Vincent Lafforgue and on Deligne's theory of Frobenius weights, combined with an existing classification of unitary spherical representations. This is a highly technical result, only seven weeks old with a single citation so far, but it earns its spot because publication in the Annals of Mathematics is itself a mark of rigorous vetting in a field where citation counts build slowly.

Next, computational biology. In Nature Methods, Can Ergen and colleagues at the University of Würzburg, the University of California Berkeley, and the Weizmann Institute of Science introduced resolVI, a computational tool for spatial transcriptomics. Spatial transcriptomics lets researchers measure RNA activity directly within intact tissue, preserving where each cell sits. A persistent problem in this field is that molecules often get assigned to the wrong cell during image segmentation, which the authors say limits analysis to predefined cell types and obscures new ones. ResolVI works downstream of any segmentation method, building a probabilistic model that corrects for this misassignment along with batch effects and other technical noise. The authors report it improves researchers' ability to distinguish cell states and detect subtle spatial expression changes. It's freely available as open-source software. What stands out here is the pace of uptake: twenty-three citations within three weeks, unusually fast for a bioinformatics tool, suggesting it's addressing a real bottleneck labs have been struggling with.

Now to the history of biology, and a correction to a long-told story. According to Science's news coverage and NPR, a new analysis pushes back on James Watson's long-standing claim that he alone first recognized the significance of Photograph 51, Rosalind Franklin's X-ray image that was key evidence for the double helix structure of DNA. The piece draws on archival material to argue Franklin's own understanding of the image has been understated in the historical record. This isn't a new experiment, it's historical reanalysis, but it has drawn attention well beyond academic circles, covered by both a science outlet and a general-audience outlet, and generating substantial discussion on Hacker News, with close to three hundred points and over a hundred comments. The source material provided focuses mainly on the headline claim itself, so we'll leave it there rather than speculate on specifics of the new archival evidence.

From biology's history to physics, though the implications touch basic biophysics. According to a Nature news piece, the STAR Collaboration, writing in the journal Science, reports what Nature's piece calls the strongest experimental evidence yet that a property called baryon number isn't carried by quarks themselves, but by structures called baryon junctions that bind the quarks together. Baryon number is the quantity conserved in protons and neutrons, and understanding what physically carries it bears on bigger questions, including why the universe ended up with more matter than antimatter after the Big Bang. This is reported as an experimental physics result from an independent research collaboration published in a peer-reviewed journal, and while it's a smaller story by social media measures, just a few Hacker News points, it was selected for challenging a textbook assumption about one of the most basic particles in nature.

Turning to cardiology, a randomized trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine addressed transcatheter tricuspid valve repair. Jörg Hausleiter and colleagues at LMU Klinikum and the German Centre for Cardiovascular Research enrolled 360 patients with symptomatic severe tricuspid regurgitation, a condition where a heart valve fails to close properly, assigning them two to one toward valve repair plus medical therapy, versus medical therapy alone. On the trial's first primary endpoint, a composite measure of death, heart failure hospitalization, and quality of life at one year, the repair group showed a win ratio of 2.42, a statistically significant result favoring the procedure. On the second endpoint, tracking death or heart failure hospitalization out to three years, just over half of the repair group avoided both outcomes, compared to about one in five in the medical-therapy-only group. Major adverse events within 30 days occurred in about 6 percent of the repair group. The authors, funded by the German Center for Cardiovascular Research among others, conclude the repair procedure was superior to medical therapy alone. This is a randomized controlled trial, the strongest form of clinical evidence, and it's already drawn nine citations in seven weeks.

Now, a corrective on AI and drug discovery. In the Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation, Shunzhou Wan and colleagues at University College London conducted an independent evaluation of Boltz-2, an AI model designed to predict protein structures and drug binding. Testing it against tens of thousands of compounds for two protein targets, they compared Boltz-2's predictions to traditional docking methods and to binding energies calculated using a physics-based method called ESMACS. The authors report only weak to moderate correlation between Boltz-2's predicted binding strength and the physics-based benchmark, and when they focused on the top 100 candidate compounds, the kind that matter most for actually picking a drug lead, they found no significant correlation at all, alongside frequent errors in how the model predicted ligand positioning. The authors conclude Boltz-2 lacks the precision needed for lead identification and argue physics-based methods remain necessary. They open by noting that, despite continuing hype, no AI-discovered drug has yet received regulatory approval. This is a peer-reviewed, independent evaluation, not a company benchmark, which is exactly why it's worth your attention.

Staying with AI, but shifting to a very different kind of source: a blog post titled "Why isn't the industry freaking out about DeepSeek 4.1 Flash?" went viral on Hacker News, drawing over eleven hundred points and nearly a thousand comments. It's worth being clear about what this is: one developer's personal, subjective account of using the model heavily across projects, not an independent benchmark or peer-reviewed study. The author claims the model is dramatically cheaper than frontier competitors, citing a large reduction in a technical component called the key-value cache that affects GPU memory costs, and argues this makes extensive AI-assisted coding sessions cost a fraction of what frontier models charge. These are the author's impressions and cost estimates, not verified lab results, and the post itself admits it is anecdotal. We include it because of the sheer scale of discussion it sparked about shifting economics in AI, not because its specific technical claims have been independently verified.

Finally, under worth reading: a guest post on Terence Tao's blog, written by Álvaro Lozano-Robledo, took on students' anxieties about whether a career in mathematics still makes sense given rapid progress in AI systems that can assist with proofs. The author, responding to messages from worried undergraduates and graduate students, argues that no one, including AI companies themselves, can currently say with confidence whether AI will surpass human mathematical research, and cautions against trusting anyone who claims certainty on the matter. He notes frontier AI companies have an interest in promoting narratives of near-term superhuman capability ahead of public offerings, and argues that despite impressive demonstrations on famous problems, the day-to-day work of mathematicians hasn't fundamentally changed yet. This is an opinion essay, not a study, but it drew over 160 Hacker News points and more than 250 comments, reflecting how live this question is in the mathematical community.

That's the briefing for today. Thanks for listening, and we'll be back with more tomorrow.

    source

    source · BioPharma Dive · Endpoints News · Fierce Biotech

    Why it's here: 8 days old; 18 Hacker News points / 17 comments
    source

Transcript

Welcome to your science briefing for Thursday, October 15th. Today we cover a brewing controversy over how AI companies are publishing mathematics, alongside new brain atlases, a physics result from deep underground, and a vaccine trial readout.

Our lead story concerns OpenAI and the mathematics community. According to Wired, the New York Times, Nature, Science, and The Verge, OpenAI posted more than seven hundred mathematical preprints to GitHub on October 6th, covering, by The Verge's count, 372 result families. OpenAI told Nature its goal is to provide tools for mathematicians and scientists, and a company spokesperson told Wired that an internal model has now resolved more than one hundred long-standing open problems, including the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem announced in September. This story has drawn coverage from five outlets across tech, general, and science press, and generated 760 points and 655 comments on Hacker News, which is why it's getting extended treatment today.

The reaction from mathematicians has been sharp. Nature quotes number theorist Alvaro Lozano-Robledo calling the volume of papers staggering, and reports some researchers describing it as a slopocalypse, even though the underlying math could turn out to be correct. Columbia's Michael Harris told Nature he considers the release illegitimate and won't be reading the papers. Oxford mathematician Ursula Martin said it amounts to, in her words, tossing the community a messy first draft and expecting them to clean it up.

Wired reports that OpenAI convened roughly 40 mathematicians in August to discuss how to handle the release, and that attendees, including Northwestern's Bryna Kra, asked the company to publish through peer-reviewed channels rather than blog posts or social media, so the community could properly digest the results. Kra told Wired that input was apparently ignored. Wired also describes a separate dispute in which NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster accused OpenAI of publishing work that overlapped with an unpublished collaboration of his; OpenAI researcher Sébastien Bubeck disputed the characterization in a public statement.

An independent advisory group called AGMAI, formed to guide these releases, had urged AI labs to publish through established academic channels and disclose details like compute costs, and specifically asked companies not to treat math results as marketing for their models. The Verge reports OpenAI says it's publishing through GitHub with citation protocols while exploring other community-hosted options.

Extending this story, Terence Tao's blog posted a statement this week from the Association for Human Mathematics, a mathematician advocacy group. According to the statement, the group argues OpenAI ignored AGMAI's central recommendation against testing advanced problems purely on internal models, and said releasing seven hundred files at once, in their words, is not a demonstration of scholarship but a demonstration of power. The post, which drew 18 points and 17 comments on Hacker News, urges mathematicians to discontinue collaboration with OpenAI. It's worth noting this is an advocacy statement, not a peer-reviewed assessment of the mathematics itself, but it captures how organized the pushback has become.

Turning to biology, two new atlases in Nature are giving researchers finer-grained maps of the brain. The first, from a team at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne led by Luca Fusar Bassini, mapped the lipid composition of the adult mouse brain at micrometer scale. The authors report that lipids cluster into what they call lipizones, biochemical territories that align with brain anatomy and connectivity, and that these lipizones reveal new structure in white matter and in pregnant mice, where the authors found white matter becomes metabolically activated and the cortex undergoes region-specific remodeling. This is a mouse study, published three weeks ago, and has already picked up eight citations; the authors describe it as a foundational resource for understanding lipids in brain disease.

The second Nature paper, from Sanan Venkatesh and colleagues at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, tackles a different problem: pinpointing which brain cell types carry genetic risk for neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. Using single-nucleus gene expression data from a multi-ancestry human cohort called PsychAD, the authors built models linking genetic variants to gene expression in specific brain cell types, then validated the associations in an independent, cross-ancestry dataset from the Million Veteran Program. The authors report thousands of gene-trait associations that bulk tissue analysis would have missed, resolved down to specific neuronal, glial, and immune cell populations. This is a human genetic and transcriptomic study, also three weeks old, with six citations so far.

In computational biology, a tool called AlphaBridge, described in the journal Structure by a team at the Netherlands Cancer Institute, addresses a practical problem created by AI structure prediction: how to evaluate the flood of predicted protein complexes coming out of tools like AlphaFold3. The authors built a web-based system that clusters interaction interfaces by confidence score and visualizes them as chord diagrams and network graphs, aiming to give researchers an automated, objective first pass before committing to more resource-intensive validation. Published six weeks ago, it's already accumulated 44 citations, a notable uptake for a bioinformatics tool, suggesting the field needed exactly this kind of triage step.

In pure mathematics, a paper in the Annals of Mathematics from Elon Lindenstrauss, a Fields Medalist at the Institute for Advanced Study, and coauthors at Johns Hopkins, proves effective equidistribution theorems with polynomial error rates for certain unipotent flows in arithmetic quotients related to the group SL2. The authors say the proof relies on a Margulis function, tools from incidence geometry, and the spectral gap of the ambient space. This is dense, technical homogeneous dynamics, the kind of result that typically accrues citations slowly; it currently has one, but its appearance in a top journal from a leading figure in the field is itself a signal of significance, offering a notable contrast to the unreviewed mass of AI-generated preprints discussed earlier.

In an AI-assisted drug discovery result, researchers at Baylor College of Medicine, writing in Nature Communications, combined large-scale proteomics with AI-based protein structure prediction to find new molecular glue compounds targeting a protein called VAV1, relevant to blood cancers and autoimmune disease. The authors report identifying a previously uncharacterized binding site, which they call a non-canonical RT-loop degron, and used a workflow combining AI structure prediction with physics-based free energy calculations to rank candidate compounds by potency. They also found that one of their compounds unexpectedly hit a second protein, LIMD1, illustrating how the same glue molecule can engage different binding motifs. This is laboratory and computational work, not yet in animals or humans, published five weeks ago with five citations.

In physics, the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment, a dark matter detector operated by a large collaboration including SLAC and Stanford, published results in Physical Review Letters searching for light dark matter particles using over five and a half tonne-years of data collected between 2023 and 2025. The collaboration reports no significant dark matter signal, allowing them to set what they call world-leading limits on certain dark matter interactions for particle masses down to five billion electron volts. But they did find something else: a signal consistent with solar neutrinos scattering coherently off atomic nuclei, at a statistical significance of four and a half sigma, which the authors call the most significant evidence yet for this process from boron-8 solar neutrinos. This is a peer-reviewed physics result, 13 weeks old, with six citations, demonstrating the detector's sensitivity to faint signals at low energies.

Finally, in biotech, Vaxcyte announced that its experimental pneumococcal vaccine, VAX-31, met its primary endpoints in a Phase 3 trial, according to the company and reporting from STAT, BioPharma Dive, Endpoints News, and Fierce Biotech. The trial randomized just over 3,500 adults aged 50 and older to receive VAX-31 or one of two approved vaccines, Pfizer's Prevnar 20 and Merck's Capvaxive. BioPharma Dive reports VAX-31 matched the comparators' effectiveness against 28 shared bacterial strains and was superior on three unique strains, though it fell short against two strains under a stricter statistical threshold. The company says the vaccine was well tolerated, with safety similar to the approved shots. This is a company announcement about a late-stage human trial, not yet a peer-reviewed publication, and two more Phase 3 studies are expected next year before any regulatory filing. Shares in the company rose sharply on the news, and analysts quoted by BioPharma Dive called the data close to a best-case outcome, though independent confirmation will have to wait for full data disclosure.

That's the briefing for today. The mathematics world's standoff with AI labs shows no sign of resolving soon, even as other corners of science quietly keep producing carefully reviewed, incrementally cited work. We'll be back tomorrow.

A roundup of a near-$8 billion Novartis licensing deal, a peer-reviewed trial restoring partial vision with optogenetics, and new frontier AI models, alongside vetted findings in genetics, genomics tools, and pure mathematics.

  1. Novartis wagers almost $8B on a Chinese biotech's RNA drugs — Endpoints News, BioPharma Dive · Biotech & pharma
    Novartis will pay Abogen Biosciences up to roughly 7.8 billion dollars for rights to an mRNA-based T cell engager technology, in a deal covered by two independent biotech trade outlets.

  4. ntSynt-viz: visualizing synteny patterns across multiple genomes — Journal of Evolutionary Biology · Computational biology & bioinformatics

    An Annals of Mathematics paper extends Mahler's method to several variables, resolving open questions about irrational numbers expressed in different numerical bases.
    Why it's here: 6 weeks old; 3 citations

  6. Boehringer, Envisagenics sign $1B multi-target oncology collaboration — Fierce Biotech · AI for biology & medicine
    Boehringer Ingelheim and AI drug-discovery company Envisagenics announced a collaboration worth up to one billion dollars to validate tumor-specific cancer targets found through RNA-splicing analysis.
    Why it's here: 20 days old; covered by 1 outlet across 1 outlet type (biotech/health trade press)
    source
  7. Claude Haiku 5.5 — anthropic.com · AI
    Anthropic released Claude Haiku 5.5, a smaller, faster model the company says costs about 75 percent less to run than its predecessor, drawing over a thousand Hacker News points.
    Why it's here: 6 days old; 1047 Hacker News points / 488 comments; fast-tracked: younger than the usual waiting period, admitted on exceptional traction
    source · Hacker News discussion
  8. Opus 5.5 agents discover two room-temperature magnetic semiconductor candidates — vals.ai · Science beyond biology
    A blog post describes AI agents running quantum simulations to propose candidate room-temperature magnetic semiconductor materials for computer memory, though the designs remain computational predictions rather than confirmed lab syntheses.
    Why it's here: 8 days old; 495 Hacker News points / 340 comments; fast-tracked: younger than the usual waiting period, admitted on exceptional traction
    source · Hacker News discussion
  9. The Future of Mathematics — What's New (Terence Tao) · Worth reading
    On Terence Tao's blog, mathematician Jeremy Avigad reflects on how mathematical practice might evolve as AI systems become capable of generating results once considered original research.

Transcript

Welcome to your briefing for Tuesday, October 13th. Today we cover a major pharma licensing deal, a peer-reviewed trial that partially restored sight in blind patients, a newly discovered mechanism of gene transfer in fruit flies, a genomics visualization tool, a result in pure mathematics, an AI-driven drug discovery partnership, a new small language model, an AI-assisted materials science search, and a reflective essay on the future of mathematics.

First, pharma. Novartis has agreed to pay the Chinese biotech Abogen Biosciences up to roughly 7.8 billion dollars for rights to its RNA drug technology, according to BioPharma Dive and Endpoints News, two independent biotech trade outlets. Of that, 575 million dollars is upfront, covering an option to license a molecule called ABO2203. This is described by Abogen as an mRNA-encoded biologic that instructs cells to produce their own T cell engagers, a type of immune therapy, rather than manufacturing those engager proteins in a lab and infusing them directly. Abogen presented early data in April from a study in patients with relapsed or refractory B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma; BioPharma Dive reports the treatment was generally well tolerated, though three patients had significant adverse events, including drops in white blood cell counts, that resolved during the trial. Novartis's biomedical research head, Fiona Marshall, called the approach in vivo production of these molecules in a company statement. BioPharma Dive notes this is one of at least a dozen such licensing deals this year between Western drugmakers and Chinese biotechs, and that Novartis is under investor pressure after several of its own drug candidates failed trials in September. This item made the cut because it's covered by two independent trade outlets and reflects a sizable industry bet.

Next, a peer-reviewed clinical result in vision restoration. A paper published October 7th in the New England Journal of Medicine, covered by STAT, Science News, and the Guardian, reports that an optogenetic gene therapy partially restored light sensitivity and some functional vision in patients with retinitis pigmentosa, a genetic disease that destroys light-sensing cells in the retina. The approach, developed by a team including Botond Roska of the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel and José-Alain Sahel of the University of Pittsburgh, uses a harmless virus to deliver genetic instructions for a light-sensitive algae protein called ChrimsonR into retinal ganglion cells, which normally relay visual signals rather than detect light directly. Patients then wear goggles that capture their surroundings and project pulses of amber light onto the retina to activate those engineered cells. Science News reports the treatment improved light sensitivity in seven of ten participants, while the Guardian reports six of ten participants had clinically meaningful improvements and four of eight who completed behavioral testing could find a doorway or follow a line. No patient could read or recognize faces. The approach requires an intact optic nerve, and researchers say restoring higher-resolution vision, such as face recognition, remains a goal for the future. This result builds on a single-patient report from 2021 and drew coverage across trade, science, and general press, prompting us to feature it a bit earlier than usual.

Now to a genuinely novel biology finding. A paper in Cell from Maya Voichek and colleagues at the Institute of Molecular Biotechnology in Vienna describes a new way that genetic elements called retrotransposons can spread between cells. Working in fruit flies, the authors report that certain of these elements can travel directly from the mother's ovary tissue into developing egg cells, something previously thought to require genes copied from retroviruses. Instead, the authors found a short protein called sORF2 that helps form physical protrusions connecting the two cell types, allowing viral-like capsids to cross over; when this protein was removed, that transmission stopped. The authors also report that similar proteins turn up in other insect retrotransposons and even in some fish and bird viruses, suggesting a broader shared mechanism. The paper has drawn seven citations in about six weeks, a sign of early attention in a niche but foundational area of genetics.

In computational biology, a paper in the Journal of Evolutionary Biology from Lauren Coombe and colleagues at BC Cancer Agency and the University of British Columbia introduces a tool called ntSynt-viz, designed to visualize synteny, meaning shared gene order, across multiple genomes at once. The authors report it produces clearer chromosome painting plots than existing tools when applied to data from fourteen human genomes and nine hoverfly genomes, and that it can also handle pangenome graphs built from sixteen fruit fly genomes. This is a practical infrastructure paper rather than a biological discovery, but it has already accumulated 22 citations in six weeks, suggesting researchers are adopting it to handle the growing pile of chromosome-scale genome assemblies.

In pure mathematics, a paper in the Annals of Mathematics by Boris Adamczewski and colleagues at Lyon 1 Université extends what's called Mahler's method, a tool from transcendence theory used to study which numbers are irrational or algebraically independent, to systems involving several variables. The authors report this lets them resolve open questions about numbers expressed in different numerical bases; for instance, they prove that no irrational real number can be automatically generated, in the technical sense used in automata theory, in two bases that don't share a common root. They also provide a new, more general proof of a classical result called Cobham's theorem. Publication in the Annals of Mathematics is itself a significant form of vetting in a field where results accumulate slowly, and the paper has three citations so far.

Turning to AI's growing role in the research pipeline: Fierce Biotech reports that Boehringer Ingelheim has signed a collaboration worth up to one billion dollars with the AI drug discovery company Envisagenics. Under the deal, announced by the companies, Boehringer will validate cancer targets identified by Envisagenics's SpliceCore platform, which uses machine learning to analyze RNA splicing, the process by which genes are cut and reassembled into different protein versions. The company says the platform screens more than 14 million splicing events to find protein versions found almost exclusively in tumors, which could make for safer, more selective drugs. Envisagenics' chief executive, Maria Pineda, told Fierce the funds will also help advance the company's own pipeline into the clinic. This is a company-announced deal, not independently verified data, but it's one of several recent partnerships, following prior tie-ups with Bristol Myers Squibb, Johnson & Johnson, and Biogen, illustrating how AI target-discovery platforms are becoming routine business in pharma.

In AI itself, Anthropic announced Claude Haiku 5.5, a smaller, faster version of its Claude model line, intended for high-volume tasks like summarization, classification, and acting as a subagent during coding work. The company says it costs around 75 percent less to run on average than its predecessor and includes an adjustable effort setting that lets users trade off cost against capability. Anthropic also says it's cutting prices on cached requests for its mid-sized Sonnet model and introducing monthly API credits for subscribers. This is a company announcement, with performance figures coming from Anthropic's own benchmarks, but it drew over a thousand points and nearly 500 comments on Hacker News within days, which is why we're covering it ahead of our usual waiting period.

Staying with AI, a write-up on vals.ai describes an experiment in which AI agents built on Anthropic's Opus 5.5 model were used to search for new magnetic semiconductor materials relevant to computer memory research. The author reports the agents proposed a new five-element compound, predicted by quantum mechanical simulations to behave as a so-called Luttinger-compensated magnet, a type of material with useful spin-sorting properties but no external magnetic field; however, the same simulations suggest its atomic structure would likely fall apart under the high temperatures needed to manufacture it. The agents separately identified an existing compound, first reported in 1999, that the author says may already satisfy many of the same requirements. It's worth stressing these are computational predictions from density functional theory simulations, not confirmed laboratory syntheses, and the write-up is a blog post rather than a peer-reviewed study. It nonetheless drew nearly 500 Hacker News points, enough to fast-track it here.

Finally, for something to read: on Terence Tao's blog, mathematician Jeremy Avigad contributed an essay reflecting on how mathematics might change as AI systems become capable of generating solutions once considered publishable results. Avigad argues that the core of mathematics isn't any particular theorem but a culture of rigorous reasoning, and suggests three paths forward: using AI to tackle harder problems, choosing bigger and more original questions that current AI systems aren't suited to pose, and finding genuinely new ways of using the technology. He draws on historical examples, including Riemann's 1854 lecture on the foundations of geometry, to argue that the most influential mathematical ideas have often come from open-ended thinking that reinforcement-learning-style systems aren't built to reward. The essay drew over 120 Hacker News points, reflecting interest in this bigger-picture question among a technical audience.

That's the briefing for today. We'll be back tomorrow with more.

    source · Hacker News discussion

    Why it's here: 6 days old; covered by 8 outlets across 3 outlet types (science press, general press, biotech/health trade press); fast-tracked: younger than the usual waiting period, admitted on exceptional traction
    source · Nature · Nature · Science (news)

Transcript

Welcome to your science briefing for Monday, October 12th. Today we cover a major pharma licensing deal, a landmark cell therapy result, several peer-reviewed advances in biology and mathematics, a contested AI announcement, and this year's Chemistry Nobel Prize.

We start with biotech and pharma. Merck has entered a collaboration with the Shanghai-based biotech SciBrunch worth up to two point one three billion dollars, according to a company release covered by Endpoints News, Fierce Biotech, and GEN. The deal gives Merck exclusive global rights to SPR2015, a preclinical, oral molecule described as a KRAS G12D inhibitor and molecular glue. KRAS is a frequently mutated gene involved in cancer growth, and the G12D variant is found in roughly thirty eight percent of pancreatic, colorectal, and lung cancer cases, according to a 2023 study cited by GEN. Merck says SPR2015 showed nanomolar antiproliferative activity in various KRAS G12D mutant cell lines in preclinical testing, with selectivity over normal KRAS cells. At the 2026 American Association for Cancer Research meeting, SciBrunch researchers presented mouse data comparing SPR2015 to another undisclosed G12D inhibitor, reporting a sixty four point seven percent objective response rate and ninety four point one percent disease control rate as a monotherapy in colorectal cancer models. One industry analyst, quoted by GEN, noted the key question is whether these preclinical properties will translate to humans, especially since competing KRAS G12D drugs from Revolution Medicines and Verastem already have early human data. Merck and SciBrunch have not disclosed a timeline for starting human trials. This item made the cut because it's been corroborated by three biotech trade outlets over the past two weeks, reflecting a broader industry push into drugging historically undruggable KRAS mutations.

Staying with biotech, Endpoints News also flagged a five-year durability result for Legend Biotech's CAR-T therapy Carvykti, suggesting it may functionally cure a subset of multiple myeloma patients. Unfortunately, the source material available to us today contains only the headline and no further detail on the study design, patient numbers, or specific outcomes. Given how thin that is, we can't say more than that this signal exists and comes from a single trade outlet; we'll follow up if more detail becomes available.

Moving to biology and biomedical research. A paper in Nature from researchers at Albert Einstein College of Medicine and University College London examined how the brain coordinates sleep across distant cortical regions. The authors identified a sparse class of inhibitory neurons, called Sst-Chodl cells, that are active during low-arousal states like slow wave sleep and largely silent during wakefulness. Unlike most inhibitory neurons, which act locally, these cells send long-range axons that reach multiple brain regions at once. In mice, the authors report that selectively activating these cells was sufficient to synchronize activity across the cortex and to induce sleep behavior. The findings suggest cortical circuits themselves can actively promote sleep, not just respond to signals from deeper brain structures. This paper is about five weeks old and has already drawn nine citations, a signal of quick interest from the field, though as always, citation counts this early are a signal, not a final verdict on impact.

Also in Nature, researchers at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Rockefeller University studied how fruit flies track odor plumes. Using a virtual reality setup for head-fixed Drosophila, the team found that flies don't simply react reflexively to odor boundaries. Instead, they use a strategy the authors call edge tracking, alternating between quick turns out of an odor plume and directed returns to its edge. Through behavioral modeling, calcium imaging, and neural perturbations, the authors show this relies on vector-based computations in a brain region called the central complex, where flies appear to store and update a memory of the direction back to the plume boundary. Specific neurons called FC2 cells, previously linked to encoding navigational goals, signaled this return direction when flies were outside the plume. The study is about twelve weeks old with nine citations so far.

In computational biology, a paper in Cell Genomics from the University of California, Santa Cruz, reconstructed the genetic ancestry of the extinct dire wolf. The authors generated two ancient genomes, one sequenced to three point four times coverage and dated to more than thirteen thousand years ago, the other at twelve point eight times coverage and more than seventy two thousand years old. Comparing these to ten living canid species, they report that roughly two-thirds of dire wolf ancestry traces to a lineage related to gray wolves, coyotes, and dholes, while the remaining third comes from a lineage near the base of the broader dog-like canine family tree. The authors say this resolves a long-standing question about where dire wolves fit on the canid family tree and adds evidence that gene flow between species after they diverged has shaped canid evolution. The paper is eleven weeks old with seven citations.

In mathematics, a paper in Inventiones Mathematicae by researchers at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and the University of Cambridge computed rational homotopy groups, a tool for classifying shapes up to continuous deformation, for diffeomorphisms of high-dimensional discs. In plain terms, the authors worked out detailed structural information about the ways a disc-shaped space can be smoothly deformed while keeping its boundary fixed, in a range of dimensions up to about one and a half times the disc's dimension. From this, they determined what they call the optimal rational concordance stable range for high-dimensional discs, and made calculations relevant to a broader topological framework known as Weiss calculus. This is a technical, foundational result in high-dimensional topology. It's fourteen weeks old with three citations, which is typical since pure math papers tend to accumulate citations slowly.

Turning to AI applied to biology, a paper in Science from Stanford University describes a system called the Virtual Biotech, a set of coordinated AI agents designed to mirror the structure of a drug research organization. A lead agent delegates scientific questions to specialized agents covering areas like statistical genetics, functional genomics, and clinical data, then integrates their findings. The authors demonstrate three uses. First, the agents analyzed outcomes from nearly fifty six thousand clinical trials and reported that drugs targeting genes specific to particular cell types were forty percent more likely to advance from Phase one to Phase two trials, forty eight percent more likely to reach the market, and showed thirty two percent fewer adverse events. Second, the system evaluated a cancer target called B7-H3 for lung cancer and proposed a drug strategy while flagging potential weaknesses. Third, it analyzed a failed ulcerative colitis trial and proposed ways to refine patient selection in future trials. The authors frame this as a tool to help human scientists move faster, with people still in the loop. This is a peer-reviewed paper, about four weeks old, with three citations so far.

Now to a widely discussed AI story. OpenAI published a post describing results from its models on mathematical problems, sharing proofs and reasoning summaries in a GitHub repository, including formal verifications in the proof-checking language Lean for many of the results. According to OpenAI, the company consulted an independent advisory group at the Institute for Advanced Study on how to responsibly share these results, and the average result they're highlighting used computing power equivalent to about three hours of their ChatGPT Pro tier. The company says it plans to fund workshops and conferences to help the math community understand and verify these results. This post is only six days old but generated over thirteen hundred points and more than fifteen hundred comments on Hacker News, reflecting intense interest and, reportedly, significant debate about how these claims should be evaluated. The source material here is a company blog post, not an independent verification, so the appropriate posture is interest paired with caution until the mathematics community reviews the specific results.

Finally, this year's Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Henri Kagan of the University of Paris-Sud and Kenso Soai of Tokyo University of Science shared the prize, announced by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, for explaining how chemical reactions can produce molecules of just one mirror-image form, a property called homochirality. According to Nature, Kagan showed in the 1980s that a small imbalance in the handedness of a catalyst can be amplified in the products of a reaction. In 1995, Soai designed a reaction, now known as the Soai reaction, in which the product of a reaction is itself a catalyst for making more of the same mirror-image form, driving the imbalance even further. NPR reports that chemist Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel committee, called it quite possibly the coolest experiment in organic chemistry. The discoveries matter because life's molecules, from DNA to amino acids, consistently favor one mirror-image form over the other, and this work helps explain how that bias could emerge from ordinary chemistry rather than needing to be built in from the start. Researchers interviewed by Nature noted that whether a similar reaction could have occurred under early Earth conditions remains an open question, since the Soai reaction doesn't work in water. Today, say both NPR and Nature, these principles underpin how chemists design catalysts used in making most modern drugs. This story was covered by at least eight outlets across science, general, and trade press, reflecting its broad significance.

That's today's briefing. Across these stories, a common theme is verification catching up with ambition, whether that means five-year clinical follow-up, independent review of AI-generated proofs, or a Nobel committee finally recognizing decades-old chemistry. Thanks for listening, and we'll be back tomorrow.

    Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for founding the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, which opened the field of neutrino astronomy.
    Why it's here: 6 days old; covered by 6 outlets across 2 outlet types (science press, general press); 582 Hacker News points / 213 comments; fast-tracked: younger than the usual waiting period, admitted on exceptional traction

  2. 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine Goes to Optogenetics, Light-Gated Ion Channels — Nature, Science (news), Guardian Science, STAT, NPR +4 more · Biology & biomedical research
    Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel share the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for developing optogenetics, the light-based tool for controlling neurons.
    Why it's here: 7 days old; covered by 9 outlets across 3 outlet types (science press, general press, biotech/health trade press); 2 Hacker News points / 1 comments; fast-tracked: younger than the usual waiting period, admitted on exceptional traction
    source · Nature · Nature · Science (news)
  3. Harmful tau spreads like self-propagating prion proteins — Nature · Biology & biomedical research
